On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 12:50:49 AM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Just don’t give any presentations using comic sans and garish color palettes.  :-p
> Seriously, though, it’s all about facilitating robust scientific inference so we’re glad
> the discussion was useful!
>
> On Nov 30, 2015, at 10:54 PM, michael burgess <jmichae...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Ok, so after reading the recommended articles and trusting your advice on what I should expect (paying attention to HDIs instead of nailing point estimates) I think this issue is solved. The astrophysical literature based off papers related to the the comic sans presentation posted earlier endorsed this Inv. Gamma prior a lot but the arguments in Gellman make more sense. Thanks all for your help and I will be sure to give some credit in the acknowledgements in the publication I'm working on.
> >
> > Cheers!
> >
> >
> >
> > On Monday, November 30, 2015 at 10:10:26 PM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > >
> > > > The beta is too small. So it is being pulled toward zero. I've seen more advanced approaches to this (Kelly (2007) if you are familiar) that nail beta well with the same data.... but there is a growing bias in beta towards zero. Just smaller than my approach here. But maybe the answer is just that, with growing error in x_obs, you can't get away from being pulled towards zero... depressing, but honest. I'll keep playing and post the papers in a few moments.
> > >
> > > I wouldn’t say it’s depressing — it’s a proper quantification of uncertainty which should
> > > be exciting!  Ultimately you don’t want to compare any posterior-derived point estimate
> > > of beta to the truth but rather the entire posterior distribution.  For example, it’s a much
> > > fairer comparison to see if a 90% credible interval (between the 5% and 95% quantiles)
> > > captures the true value of beta most of the time.  In the large measurement error case
> > > the posterior mean of beta might be drawn to zero but the posterior itself will widen to
> > > reflect the growing uncertainty, which is exactly what we want!  The only way to get
> > > better inferences is to introduce more information, and if that data can’t be measured
> > > any better than that would have to mean a different likelihood or priors.
> > >
> > > Kelly (2007) is an entirely different beast which uses a mixture of Gaussian amongst
> > > other bells and whistles, so it’s really a proper comparison.  You can build this model
> > > in Stan no problem and then you should at least get consistent results (although you
> > > might not — HMC tends to identify bad fits much better than Random Walk Metropolis
> > > and Gibbs).

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been working on the model. I think aspects of my original re-purposing of Bob's code were flawed. I believe I've fixed most of those errors, but now I'm struggling with how I can vectorize my loops. Without such vectorization, things are still running fairly slow.

I'm attaching the code I have right now, which is working. I've gained a lot of speed from past suggestions. I'm still working on the vectorization. In the Stan model I've commented out large section in the model block -- those sections are my failed attempts at vectorizing the preceding for() loops. The functions are all for the vectorized form, and I don't currently use them in the for() loops.

The whole problem for me can probably be summarized as the need to reformulate the following functions (Bob's) for use when psi and theta not just among species, but among species and sites:

real lp_observed(int x, int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta) {
    return log_inv_logit(logit_psi) + binomial_logit_log(x, K, logit_theta);
}
real lp_unobserved(int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta) {
    return log_sum_exp(lp_observed(0, K, logit_psi, logit_theta), log1m_inv_logit(logit_psi));
}
real lp_never_observed(int J, int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta, real Omega) {
    real lp_unavailable;
    real lp_available;
    lp_unavailable <- bernoulli_log(0, Omega);
    lp_available <- bernoulli_log(1, Omega) + J * lp_unobserved(K, logit_psi, logit_theta);
    return log_sum_exp(lp_unavailable, lp_available);
}
​
Terms involving Omega should only be incremented once per species, I believe. So the first term in lp_available <- bernoulli_log(1, Omega) + J * lp_unobserved(K, logit_psi, logit_theta); must be separated from the second, and the second has to be first be summed among all T,J for a species before being added to the first term. That's why I use the lp_available_pt1 vector in my current iterative form of the Never Observed species.

I should mention that I think my vectorized version is wrong because I'm getting a different answer with the same seed. When I initially said I'd tested my model, I didn't mean the exact Stan encoding per se, but rather the general structure (and I'd tested what I had written in JAGS). Things have been reformulated quite a bit now, so it's less clear what's right or wrong.

I'll post back if I figure something out, but I've been struggling with this lately.

-Ryan

messages.body_plain:
Unless you can get things into vectorized probability functions
or simple matrix operations, there's not much else you can do to
vectorize.

The other alternative is to compute sufficient statistics and/or
turn things like multiple Bernoullis into binomials.

Another avenue of optimization is to reuse shared expressions.
It's even worthwhile to build data structures up to cache the
intermediate results if they can be reused.  For instance, if
there are two random effects with M and N levels, building
the M x N combined table and indexing into that rather than adding
each time.

If you can post a currently working version of the model, I might
have more concrete suggestions.

- Bob

> On Nov 30, 2015, at 8:52 PM, Ryan Batt <bat...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> I'm attaching the code I have right now, which is working. I've gained a lot of speed from past suggestions. I'm still working on the vectorization. In the Stan model I've commented out large section in the model block -- those sections are my failed attempts at vectorizing the preceding for() loops. The functions are all for the vectorized form, and I don't currently use them in the for() loops.
>
> The whole problem for me can probably be summarized as the need to reformulate the following functions (Bob's) for use when psi and theta not just among species, but among species and sites:
>
> real lp_observed(int x, int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta) {
>     return log_inv_logit(logit_psi) + binomial_logit_log(x, K, logit_theta);
> }
> real lp_unobserved(int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta) {
>     return log_sum_exp(lp_observed(0, K, logit_psi, logit_theta), log1m_inv_logit(logit_psi));
> }
> real lp_never_observed(int J, int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta, real Omega) {
>     real lp_unavailable;
>     real lp_available;
>     lp_unavailable <- bernoulli_log(0, Omega);
>     lp_available <- bernoulli_log(1, Omega) + J * lp_unobserved(K, logit_psi, logit_theta);
>     return log_sum_exp(lp_unavailable, lp_available);
> }
>
> ​
> Terms involving Omega should only be incremented once per species, I believe. So the first term in lp_available <- bernoulli_log(1, Omega) + J * lp_unobserved(K, logit_psi, logit_theta); must be separated from the second, and the second has to be first be summed among all T,J for a species before being added to the first term. That's why I use the lp_available_pt1 vector in my current iterative form of the Never Observed species.
>
> I should mention that I think my vectorized version is wrong because I'm getting a different answer with the same seed. When I initially said I'd tested my model, I didn't mean the exact Stan encoding per se, but rather the general structure (and I'd tested what I had written in JAGS). Things have been reformulated quite a bit now, so it's less clear what's right or wrong.
>

Thanks Bob. The current model produces “reasonable” results when fed larger data sets (5 species isn’t very many!). I’ll work on adapting old methods for verifying these models.

If I have a statement like bernoulli_log(1, Omega)*D, is it faster/ correct to switch it to binomial_log(D, D, Omega) ? Similar question for increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1, Omega) * N).

I’ll report back once I’ve verified my current Stan model. Thank you so much.
​

-Ryan

>
> Another avenue of optimization is to reuse shared expressions.
> It's even worthwhile to build data structures up to cache the
> intermediate results if they can be reused.  For instance, if
> there are two random effects with M and N levels, building
> the M x N combined table and indexing into that rather than adding
> each time.
>

> have more concrete suggestions.
>

In the Stan model I've commented out large section in the model block -- those sections are my failed attempts at vectorizing the preceding for() loops. > >
> > real lp_observed(int x, int K, real logit_psi, real logit_theta) {

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sachin,

1. The positive_ordered type doesn't have range constraints. If you look at the Stan reference guide, you can find it in the BNF grammars (in the Modeling Language Syntax section).
2. If it were to be allowed, it would be before the brackets: positive_ordered<lower=1/max(y), upper=1/min(y)>[k] (but this won't work)
3. There are lots of ways to accomplish this in Stan. One of the ways is to build the transform yourself. Another could be to use a simplex and each value could represent the difference between two lambdas.

Hopefully that helps.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
One way to use a simplex to generate
a positive ordered K-vector lambda that falls in
the interval (a, b) is as follows:

  parameters {
    simplex[K + 1] theta;
    ...
  }
  transformed parameters {
    positive_ordered[K] lambda;
    ...

    lambda <- a + head(cumulative_sum(theta), K) * (b - a);
    ...
  }

You can then use a uniform prior on kappa and a Dirichlet(alpha)
prior on kappa, which is nice because it'll control spacing.
The prior alpha can be used to control how uniform the spacing will
be.

To see how the cumulative sum works, take K=3, so we
generate a (K+1) simplex such as

 (0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4)

Its cumulative sum is

 (0.2, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0)

The first K elements are picked out by the head (0.2, 0.3, 0.6),
and then those are multiplied by (b - a), and then you add
a.

  (a + (b-a) * 0.2, a + (b-a) * 0.3, a + (b - a) * 0.6)

It's all nice and symmetric and you don't need any Jacobians anywhere.

I have no idea how well it'll work in practice, though, so please
report back if you try it!

We don't have good prior recommendations for these cases yet, either.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
messages.subject_clean: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 30, 2015 at 10:23:29 PM UTC+2, Xulong Wang wrote:

> Can I generate a null distribution of the WAIC by shuffling the genotype of each SNP (permutation), from which to compute a p-value for each of the real WAIC?

Yes, you can. This way will get some idea how big difference in WAIC is likely to be significant, but making independent models for each SNP is bad idea.

> Also, given that the full posterior distribution of each SNP's effect size was obtained by sampling, can I simply use the 95% CI and not worry about the multiple comparison issue at all?

If you make independent models, you need to worry about the multiple comparison.

It would be better to make one hierarchical model for all SNPs. Hierarchcial model with 1 million SNPs is challenging, but here are couple papers
http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0049445
http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0029115
and code
http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/bmagwa/
(unfortunately this is not possible yet with Stan)

If the hierarchical model is good, then you don't need to worry about the multiple comparison (see on Andrew's papers).

On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 7:17:13 AM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> With more than 2 models to compare, it would make sense to fit some sort of hierarchical model to the Waic output; we’ve discussed this idea but have never done it.

It's better to make hierarchical model for SNPs than for WAIC output. Making a hierarchical model for WAIC output would be as difficult as for SNP data, but less efficient as you need to make first the independent models, and WAIC summary will discard information compared to the original data.

Aki

On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 12:36:17 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Right, your posterior captures all of the true correlations!
> The problem here isn’t estimation, it’s uncertainty — you
> just don’t have enough data to inform the correlations
> all that well.

What Mike says is true, although there is the additional issue that if the true correlation matrix has 0.6 for all the off-diagonal elements and your prior on the (Cholesky factor of the) correlation matrix is much greater than 1, then the prior information you are adding to the model --- that the correlations are probably small --- is not aligned with the data-generating process. In that situation you need even more data to get point estimates of the correlations that are close to 0.6.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 12:07:03 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't know multinomial probit --- is there not an equivalent for
> softmax to normalize the probabilities?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_probit

Multinomial probit and multinomial logit (basically a softmax thing) are fundamentally different in that the former does not assume that the errors are uncorrelated / independent across outcome categories. Doing MCMC for a multinomial probit model is very difficult with either a Gibbs sampler or Stan.

Ben

Dear Bob,

after running the schools data with the non-centered hierarchical model (as suggested)  the efficiency in terms of effective sample size of iterations increased by a factor 2 to 3. The results of the centered and non-centered models were very similar. I checked the convergence behaviour with traceplots visually and using Rhat values  (all relevant parameters < 1.02), which showed good mixing of four chains of both approaches. However, also the non-centered model gave a low number (< 20) of divergent transitions when running with adept_delta of 0.8.

What is the best way to reduce divergent transitions? At the moment it seems using a non-centered model and setting adept_delta to 0.99 is the preferred solution.

What do you (or others) think?

Best, Wilmar

If you can get them to converge, they should definitely both give you
the same posterior (to within MCMC std error, of course).

want to set a stepsize (name of R control parameter) lower than the default.
I have a feeling we're going to be changing our default at some point to make
it lower.

You might also be able to control divergence with tighter priors.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This is applicable to RStan, though it's a more general issue. In short, I'd like more information about what is happening as the model runs. (verbose=TRUE doesn't give me the information I'd like.)

RSATN feature request details;
When I run a complex model, after compiling (which it doesn't announce,) it tells me SAMPLING FOR MODEL '[name here]' NOW,
(Here; https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/blob/2cf7e0720a44a57ee75e23ef802d9ba6063a1c0a/rstan/rstan/R/stanmodel-class.R at line 532)
then it (sometimes) waits a significant amount of time before *beginning* to sample.

I'd prefer a few more informational messages that inform me what is taking a long time. Before sampling, in non-verbose mode, it could tell me it was parsing data, (line 373) then compiling (line 388).
(ie. "Parsing Input Data", "Compiling Stan model to executable" - I could potentially make these changes on Github myself, it this is an OK thing to add to RStan.)

Stan Feature Requests, also - perhaps less simple to address;
After compiling, it's no longer an RStan issue, it's Stan itself; I get no information for an extended period, about 5 minutes with my big models even when they run, after it says Sampling, but before it says "Iteration:  1/n". I'm very unclear about what is causing this to go slowly, and think that (at least using verbose mode) it could allow for some more transparency into what is happening with the sampler, though I'm not familiar with that code.
Also, during the model run itself, it's probably doing tons of leapfrog steps, etc - and I'd be happy to have a "super-verbose" mode that told me what was happening in a bit more detail this; I can have it tell me about each iteration, but it seems during runtime that's the limit of how much detail I can get during the run. (At least via RStan.)

Thanks,
David

messages.subject: Re: stan and distributed computing
messages.subject_clean: stan and distributed computing
messages.body_plain:
The r-bloggers tutorial seems like a good way to set up a single remote EC2 machine with RStan. Following that, you can use any of the regular Stan models via command line RStan on that remote machine - it's not distributing the analysis among multiple machines, though - that would be harder.

You can then run one chain per EC2 computer, and combine them afterwards; how to do this is detailed here; https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/c8wb87yQkPc/Cb7mWSDgeWkJ (The task of sampling each chain doesn't parallelize, at least in the current architecture,, so it's not really useful to have a larger network except to sample more chains.)

Cheers,
David

call, so this is your best proxy for “total function evaluations”.

On Tuesday, 1 December 2015 15:56:53 UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> One way to use a simplex to generate
> a positive ordered K-vector lambda that falls in
> the interval (a, b) is as follows:
>
>   parameters {
>     simplex[K + 1] theta;
>     ...
>   }
>   transformed parameters {
>     positive_ordered[K] lambda;
>     ...
>
>     lambda <- a + head(cumulative_sum(theta), K) * (b - a);
>     ...
>   }
>
> You can then use a uniform prior on kappa and a Dirichlet(alpha)
> prior on kappa, which is nice because it'll control spacing.
> The prior alpha can be used to control how uniform the spacing will
> be.
>
> To see how the cumulative sum works, take K=3, so we
> generate a (K+1) simplex such as
>
>  (0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4)
>
> Its cumulative sum is
>
>  (0.2, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0)
>
> The first K elements are picked out by the head (0.2, 0.3, 0.6),
> and then those are multiplied by (b - a), and then you add
> a.
>
>   (a + (b-a) * 0.2, a + (b-a) * 0.3, a + (b - a) * 0.6)
>
> It's all nice and symmetric and you don't need any Jacobians anywhere.
>
> I have no idea how well it'll work in practice, though, so please
> report back if you try it!
>
> We don't have good prior recommendations for these cases yet, either.
>
> - Bob

> On Dec 1, 2015, at 8:16 PM, Sachinthaka Abeywardana <sachin.ab...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> So I made the model as Bob suggested and looks like:
> parameters {
>  simplex[k] pi;
>  simplex[k+1] theta;
> }
> transformed parameters{
>     positive_ordered[k] lambda;
>     lambda <- a + head(cumulative_sum(theta), k) * (b - a);
> }
> model {
>  lambda~exponential(1);
>         ....
> }
>
> (The entire model is attached in the files below).
>
> So I have a few questions on this even though it works:

I'm glad it works.

> 1. Is it valid to do lambda~exponential(1). The reason I ask this is because lambda depends on theta (a simplex). Also isn't the model going to try to put a uniform distribution on theta, even though I specified the prior on lambda?

What matters if the final log density.  Theta is
involved in both a default uniform prior over the simplex,
plus the distribution on lambda, which is defined in terms
of theta.  Changing theta affects the value of lambda, which
in turn affects the exponential distribution's contribution
to the log density.

> Basically how does stan consolidate the fact that it has an exponential prior and the restrictions placed by the transformed parameters block (a rough explanation would be fine).

The way it really works is through HMC.  There's an algorithm
section in the manual.

> 2. I got the following warning and not sure what it means:
> Warning (non-fatal):
> Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
> Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
>     lambda ~ exponential(...)

This you have to worry about.  Hence the warning.

Because you apply a change of variables, you have to apply
a Jacobian adjustment.  That's also described thoroughly in
the manual.

In this case, you're lucky, because a and b are constants
and the cumulative sum has a unit Jacobian determinant, so it's
a constant linear transform of a unit Jacobian, so there's no
affect on the posterior from the change of variables.

So you don't need to do anything.

I still think the Dirichlet on the bins and maybe an exponential
on the overall scale makes a lot of sense here, especially if
these are cutpoints for an ordinal regression.

> 3. Numerical problems:
> validate transformed params: lambda is not a valid ordered vector. The element at 2 is 0.00089928, b     2
> validate transformed params: lambda is not a valid ordered vector. The element at 2 is 3.72184, but      1
> Does the above mean that there were 3 numerical problems. Apologies if I was not meant to ask this on the

Looks like your response got cut off here.

How often does this turn up?  I don't see how lambda can fail
to be an ordered vector.  Is a < 0 perhaps?

- Bob

>
>
>
> On Tuesday, 1 December 2015 15:56:53 UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> One way to use a simplex to generate
> a positive ordered K-vector lambda that falls in
> the interval (a, b) is as follows:
>
>   parameters {
>     simplex[K + 1] theta;
>     ...
>   }
>   transformed parameters {
>     positive_ordered[K] lambda;
>     ...
>
>     lambda <- a + head(cumulative_sum(theta), K) * (b - a);
>     ...
>   }
>
> You can then use a uniform prior on kappa and a Dirichlet(alpha)
> prior on kappa, which is nice because it'll control spacing.
> The prior alpha can be used to control how uniform the spacing will
> be.
>
> To see how the cumulative sum works, take K=3, so we
> generate a (K+1) simplex such as
>
>  (0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4)
>
> Its cumulative sum is
>
>  (0.2, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0)
>
> The first K elements are picked out by the head (0.2, 0.3, 0.6),
> and then those are multiplied by (b - a), and then you add
> a.
>
>   (a + (b-a) * 0.2, a + (b-a) * 0.3, a + (b - a) * 0.6)
>
> It's all nice and symmetric and you don't need any Jacobians anywhere.
>
> I have no idea how well it'll work in practice, though, so please
> report back if you try it!
>
> We don't have good prior recommendations for these cases yet, either.
>
> - Bob
>

> > lambda[1]~exponetial(1) 1(lambda[1]\in[a,b])
> > lambda[2]~exponetial(1) 1(lambda[2]\in[a,lambda[1]]) ...
> > lambda[k]~exponetial(1) 1(lambda[k]\in[a,lambda[k-1]])
> > where [a,b] are the higher and lower limits.

> >
> > S

> > Programming the transform oneself could be a lot of work and it would probably slow down the computation.  A simplex would work (if the simplex variable is x, then then ordered variable is just “lower” + (“upper”- “lower”) * cumulative sum of x, and I assume Stan has a cumulative sum function.  Or it’s possible that the upper and lower constraints should really be soft in any case (I’m thinking this because it seems unusual to define a variable with data-based constraints).

> >> 3. There are lots of ways to accomplish this in Stan. One of the ways is to build the transform yourself. Another could be to use a simplex and each value could represent the difference between two lambdas.

hi

I also work on a cluster with Python 26, but it's a good practice not to work with a system Python rather in a virtual environment (so that e.g.  upgrades to system don't affect your project)

In my experience, installing Continuum's Anaconda distribution (it's free) is the easiest route. You can install to home folder, source the environment and pip install pystan (which will handle dependencies if any aren't in Anaconda distribution). If you have space quota, try the miniconda installer, where you only install what's necessary.

hope this helps,

marmaduke

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gustaf and Markus,

Sorry -- I completely missed the first message.

In Stan, we currently have a non-stiff solver. (Boost's 5th order Runga Kutta.) When parameter values are very large or very small, we're finding that even systems that are usually non-stiff may get into stiff regions.

We are currently working to get a stiff solver into Stan, but until that happens, one workaround is to put a reject statement within the system function when the parameters are very large / small. Although this puts a discontinuity in the overall Stan program, it's still better than having the integrator be stuck. Another workaround would be to put more into the model: better priors, better parameter declarations, etc.

For concreteness, after definig alpha_ab, you could do something like:

        if (alpha_ab > 10000)
          reject("alpha_ab is too large: ", alpha_ab);

On Thu, Dec 3, 2015 at 7:28 AM, Markus Gesmann <markus....@googlemail.com> wrote:

> Hi Gustaf,
>
> Did you resolve the issue with the Lotka-Volterra model?
> I tried exactly the same this morning and run into the same problem.
>
> Thanks
>
> Markus
>
>
> On Friday, 17 April 2015 14:50:27 UTC+1, Gustaf Rydevik wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I have implemented a simple Lotka-Volterra type equation as a function in stan as follows:
> > -----
> > functions {
> >       real[] lv(real t,
> >                  real[] y,
> >                  real[] theta,
> >                  real[] x_r,
> >                  int[] x_i) {
> >         real alpha_ab;
> >         real beta_ab;
> >         real alpha_na;
> >         real beta_na;
> >         real dydt[2];
> >
> >         alpha_ab<-theta[1];
> >         beta_ab<-theta[2];
> >         alpha_na<-theta[3];
> >         beta_na<-theta[4];
> >
> >         dydt[1] <- alpha_ab*y[2]-beta_ab*y[1];
> >         dydt[2] <- y[2]*(alpha_na-beta_na*y[1]);
> >         return dydt;
> > } }
> > ----
> > (full code is  attached)
> > This works great for generating synthetic data with a known starting set of variables. However, when trying to estimate the thetas using those synthetic data,
> > the sampler quickly runs into problems. When using print to debug, it seems as if integrate_ode stalls for v.large/small parameter values. In the last run, the sampler picked values
> > of
> >
> > theta<-c(1.00422e+07,9.17141e-22,2.23805e+30,1.31472e-32)
> > y0<-c(7.19909,531.881)
> >
> > ,just before the call to integrate_ode, and then nothing happened. Feeding these parameter values to the synthetic data generator also results in a stalled stan.
> > I suspect that the problem is the combination of large and small values, and numerical issues related to that. What would be the best way of solving this issue? Putting a hard range limit on the thetas and y0?  checking for reasonable parameter values in an iff statement before the integration call? Some other way of informing the sampler that extreme values will be a problem?
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Gustaf

messages.subject_clean: Using Stan for large simulation (repeated calling)
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Ben and Krzysztof for your reply, it is now much much faster!

On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 4:00:41 PM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 8:42:27 AM UTC-5, Craig Wang wrote:
> > My question is: I'm going to call the same *.stan file 1,000 times for different simulated data, is there a way to only call the C++ translation once to save time?
>
> Yes, in RStan and PyStan. In RStan, it should not compile the same model repeatedly within the same R session, but you can have it not compile repeatedly across R sessions by first calling
>
> rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
>
> In both RStan and PyStan, you can pass an existing object produced by stan() to the fit argument of stan() to use the same model with different data.
>
> > sample code:
> >
> > for (i in 1:1000){
> >   dat <- data[[i]]
> >   m2 <- stan(file="model.stan", data=dat,iter=100000, chains=1,thin=10)
> >   var[i]<-1-mean(m2@sim$samples[[1]]$var)
> >   }
>
> With Stan, we do not recommend doing 100000 iterations, one chain, or thinning like you might do with a Gibbs sampler or Metropolis-Hastings. The default arguments are more than fine the vast majority of the time. You should read about the differences between how Stan does MCMC relative to a Gibbs sampler or Metropolis-Hastings before doing a bunch of simulations. Also, we do not recommend using syntax like @sim$samples[[1]]$. Use mean(extract(m2, pars = "var", permuted = FALSE)) or something.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Complex model, slow warmup, how to diagnose?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Complex model, slow warmup, how to diagnose?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

On Fri, Dec 4, 2015 at 3:06 PM, David Manheim <davidm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Another idea; does using local variables in the model block require less sampling than having them in the transformed parameters section? (This isn't clear from the manual; I have about 20 variables that have derivatives computed when I try that, but a lot more transformed parameters output from the ODE model.)

No. There are very minor differences between declaring and defining a variable in transformed parameters or as a local variable within the model block. The differences:
- transformed parameters are checked for validity
- transformed parameters are output; local variables are not
The second point might make a difference if output is a bottleneck, but doesn't really affect Stan.

Regarding "requiring less sampling" -- I think you're misinterpreting what a Stan program does. A Stan program defines data, (constrained) parameters, and how to compute the joint probability function of the data and the parameters. Under the hood, Stan takes the constrained parameters and unconstrains them; that's changing the space and maps to -inf to inf. Stan also accounts for the change of variables and includes the Jacobians for the transforms automatically. (The program also generates a version without the Jacobians, but for NUTS, we use the one with the Jacobians.)

Conceptually, if you think of what happens at a single leapfrog step:
- the data are known
- the parameters are known (they've already been "sampled")
- all that's left to do is calculate the log probability function of the data and the parameters (unnormalized is fine)

Outside of the log probability function, NUTS then figures out how to pick the next set of parameter values. Once it does that, it does the same thing above.

The reason sampling is unaffected by the decision to put variables in transformed parameters or local variables is because the work is the same to calculate the log probability function.

Hopefully that makes some sense and helps.

>
>
> On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 12:02:13 PM UTC-8, David Manheim wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I'm seeing really slow warmup; I suspect that rescaling or changing the model structure somewhere could help, but the models is fairly complex, and I'm unsure where to start.

Slow warmup isn't necessarily problematic. Can you calibrate? What do you consider "really slow" and "fairly complex"?

The natural place to start is simpler. Start with something that works and then build up. Start with simulated data under the same assumptions as your model and then move towards working with real data that don't have the same generative mechanism.

> > One possibility is the "small" factors in the ODE; I rescaled them for sampling, but then un-scaled them when input to the ODE Solver; is that going to be a problem? (they are range-restricted to be positive, and are near 0 - but they should be near 0.)

If you're playing with ODEs, then this adds another complication. We currently have a non-stiff solver in Stan that isn't that great with stiff problems. For now, one thing you can do is put a reject() statement within the ODE if the parameters are haywire. This would prevent it getting stuck within the ODE solver.

We're working on getting a stiff solver into Stan.

> >
> > Another is correlated parameters; is there a way to figure out where this is a problem? (Or what variables I may want to scale or shift that are leading to this?)
> >
> >
> > Basically, is there a how-to for this, or is the answer that there are no heuristics that have been developed?

>
> On 3, I need to figure out whether my posterior is proper; the prior is proper, but conditional on data, conceivably it is not, right? If that's true I'm unsure I can guarantee a proper posterior.

I should have been more careful about what I wrote---sure improper posteriors are a problem but a more likely computational problem is that your priors are too weak.  As an example try to guess what appropriate priors are in a logistic regression with five coefficients:

logit(y_i) = B_0 + B_1 + B_2 + B_3 + B_4

Yeah, make them all similar---there's something specific about what Stan expects, maybe -1 to 1 works best... then transform to whathever scales you need. messages.body_plain:
Hi, just looking for some clarification.  This bit from the Stan manual (2.8.0) is not making sense to me:

> Our final recommendation is to give the correlation matrix Ω an LKJ prior with shape ν ≥ 1,
>
> Ω ∼ LKJcorr(ν).
>
> The LKJ correlation distribution is defined in Section 50.1, but the basic idea for mod- eling is that as ν increases, the prior increasingly concentrates around the unit corre- lation matrix (i.e., favors less correlation among the components of βj ). At ν = 1, the LKJ correlation distribution reduces to the identity distribution over correlation ma- trices. The LKJ prior may thus be used to control the expected amount of correlation among the parameters βj .

I think this means that v=1 is all kinds of correlation matrices possible (some sort of uninformative) and large v is suggesting mostly uncorrelated variables.... is there a way of suggesting that all the variables will be highly correlated? That seems to be something allowed for but not encouraged by v=1... sorry about the loose language.

The background is that I have a model that I want to make into a discrete mixture, but I don't want to figure out exactly how many mixture components there are so I was thinking of adding extra and constraining them using correlation.  I think the horseshoe priors paper does this sort of thing  so I have a lead on sorting this out but I'd appreciate any pointers.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Issues sampling with horseshoe prior
messages.subject_clean: Issues sampling with horseshoe prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been having some issues with implementation of the horseshoe prior in Stan.

Using half-cauchy priors for both the local and global scale parameters results in difficult sampling (slow sampling, divergent transitions even with high acceptance rate and low step-size). Re-parameterizations of the cauchy helps but does not resolve this issue.

After much exploration of the posterior samples, the issue seems to occur when the global scale parameter approximates 0.  Under this situation, the local scale for the relevant parameters is forced to extreme values far in the tails of the cauchy. Changing the priors on the scale parameters to student_t(3, 0, 1) alleviates the sampling issues, but results in lower shrinkage of less-relevant parameters towards zero.

I was wondering if anyone has experienced this issue and could offer guidance. In particular, I am thinking of using a boundary avoiding prior (such as a gamma(2, _) per BDA) on the global scale parameter to avoid this degenerate case. Or is it preferable to stick to using student_t priors rather than the cauchy?

Thanks in advance,

Thanks for the follow up.  The original question was too tough for

We recommend against uniform priors on closed intervals unless
the intervals arise from a "physical" constraint (in the way that (0,1) is a
constraint for bernoulli or binomial parameters).  Instead of
uniform(-20, 20), assuming you expect values up to 20, would be to
have normal(0, 10) on an unconstrained parameter.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Looking for help with the performance of an occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Looking for help with the performance of an occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
OK, I've verified the model. I wasn't getting great results before because of a bug in a data-input formatting function I wrote. Oops.

Sorry this took so long, I wanted to do my best to make sure I could honestly say the model is correct and working.

I'm attaching an updated, minimal, all-in-one R script (contains data, Stan model, R code for running and timing). The data are real, but very small. If desired, I can share a larger data set of simulated data where we'll know the answer. I'd be happy to share some of the code I used to verify the model (although I'd have to clean that code up a bit, just to make it readable for others).

I mentioned this in my first message, but I'd like to reiterate that although I believe the results of this model will be ecologically meaningful, I intend to make 2 'enhancements' to the model:
year- and/or site-varying parameters (hierarchical). This depends on how good the covariates are at pulling out space-time differences in occupancy
make the model of a dynamic flavor, whereby colonization and persistence terms are modelled. I know that Bob has graciously shared a simple version of such a model in the past.

One thing I've noticed during my testing is that I don't have to run a Stan model for very many iterations to get close to reasonable results. Honestly, with simulated data and this particular model, I'm finding that ~50 iterations gets be in the ballpark. In fact, I can usually figure out if the model is 'working' if I do ~20. That's orders of magnitude fewer iterations than I would do in JAGS for similar feel of accuracy.

Is there any standard expectation for the number of iterations I should run the Stan model? If I put in a paper that I ran my model for 200 iterations, a reviewer used to BUGS or JAGS would probably question the choice (if I didn't explain effective sample size, that I'm using Stan, etc). What should I consider to be in the ballpark of 'normal' for number of iterations? this point is germane to the performance of the occupancy model, because "performance" is really about "how long it takes for the model to finish", which obviously depends on # iterations. As Bob briefly alluded to, and is implied by extensive discussions here and elsewhere about "effective sample size", perhaps the easiest way to improve my definition of "performance" is to run the model for fewer iterations.

I would certainly appreciate more feedback or tips on how to improve the speediness/ accuracy (!)/ performance of this model. But in the past ~10 days (since original post), I've really become less worried after making the efficiency improvements thus far (thanks all!) and after realizing that I probably don't need 1000's of iterations.

-Ryan

p.s. When I do 20-50 iterations, there's usually a couple parameters here and there that weren't even close to converging; these are typically some of the Psi parameters (or Theta), and there's one of those for each site-year-species (a lot). Just thought I'd point out that there are obvious problems with so few iterations. Nonetheless, most parameters are pretty close to true values by that time.

messages.subject: Re: Issues sampling with horseshoe prior
messages.subject_clean: Issues sampling with horseshoe prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

We discuss this issue and Hierarchical Shrinkage priors with t_3 in
http://arxiv.org/abs/1508.02502
It is possible that there would be less shrinkage, but more likely the difference is that there will be some shrinkage for more parameters. See the figures in our paper. We didn't observe practical difference between Horseshoe and Hierarchical Shrinkage with t_3. We use the more generic term Hierarchical Shrinkage, since with t_3 the shrinkage curve does not anymore have the horseshoe shape.

Aki

On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 11:57:00 PM UTC+2, Matt Espe wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I have been having some issues with implementation of the horseshoe prior in Stan.
>
> Using half-cauchy priors for both the local and global scale parameters results in difficult sampling (slow sampling, divergent transitions even with high acceptance rate and low step-size). Re-parameterizations of the cauchy helps but does not resolve this issue.
>
> After much exploration of the posterior samples, the issue seems to occur when the global scale parameter approximates 0.  Under this situation, the local scale for the relevant parameters is forced to extreme values far in the tails of the cauchy. Changing the priors on the scale parameters to student_t(3, 0, 1) alleviates the sampling issues, but results in lower shrinkage of less-relevant parameters towards zero.
>
> I was wondering if anyone has experienced this issue and could offer guidance. In particular, I am thinking of using a boundary avoiding prior (such as a gamma(2, _) per BDA) on the global scale parameter to avoid this degenerate case. Or is it preferable to stick to using student_t priors rather than the cauchy?
>
> Thanks in advance,
>
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Looking for help with the performance of an occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
> One thing I've noticed during my testing is that I don't have to run a Stan model for very many iterations to get close to reasonable results. Honestly, with simulated data and this particular model, I'm finding that ~50 iterations gets be in the ballpark. In fact, I can usually figure out if the model is 'working' if I do ~20. That's orders of magnitude fewer iterations than I would do in JAGS for similar feel of accuracy.

Yup, HMC is fast.  One thing to be careful about is that while HMC does converge
really fast, our adaptation may not be as fast.  So if your parameters have very
different scales then it’s better to run longer warmup to learn a good metric to
standardize all of those scales.  But if your parameters are all similarly scaled
then you can get away with less warmup.

> Is there any standard expectation for the number of iterations I should run the Stan model? If I put in a paper that I ran my model for 200 iterations, a reviewer used to BUGS or JAGS would probably question the choice (if I didn't explain effective sample size, that I'm using Stan, etc). What should I consider to be in the ballpark of 'normal' for number of iterations? this point is germane to the performance of the occupancy model, because "performance" is really about "how long it takes for the model to finish", which obviously depends on # iterations. As Bob briefly alluded to, and is implied by extensive discussions here and elsewhere about "effective sample size", perhaps the easiest way to improve my definition of "performance" is to run the model for fewer iterations.

For convergence you want to quote something like R-hat.
For statistical power you want to quote ESS.
For performance you want to quote ESS / time (or time / ESS).

Raw numbers of iterations is completely meaningless and so
is not helpful in any discussion.  If editors give you crap about
this don’t hesitate to contact us and we can help push back
against poor MCMC understanding.

> p.s. When I do 20-50 iterations, there's usually a couple parameters here and there that weren't even close to converging; these are typically some of the Psi parameters (or Theta), and there's one of those for each site-year-species (a lot). Just thought I'd point out that there are obvious problems with so few iterations. Nonetheless, most parameters are pretty close to true values by that time.

Did you full non-center the model?  This could be a big
improvement.

messages.subject_clean: Autoregressive ordered probit in Stan

On Saturday, December 5, 2015 at 8:31:20 AM UTC-5, Oskar Knapik wrote:
> I am new user of Stan. I wonder if it is possible to implement autoregressive ordered probit model as it is in https://mediatum.ub.tum.de/doc/1097570/file.pdf

Yes, such a model can be expressed in the Stan language. However,
It is tedious to specify the constraints on the latent variables, especially when there are more than two categories
Even when you do that, it is very difficult to get Stan to sample efficiently due to the dependence of the latent variables on the unknown common parameters

At least for the application in that paper, I would question whether the ordered probit likelihood is appropriate. Although it is true that the prices can only change by discrete amounts, it is still a ratio-scale variable rather than something that is merely ordinal.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Questiion about half-Cauchy priors
messages.body_plain:
Kent,

The default in Stan is to provide uniform (or “flat”) priors on parameters over their
legal values as determined by their declared constraints. A parameter declared with-
out constraints is thus given a uniform prior on (−∞, ∞) by default, whereas a scale
parameter declared with a lower bound of zero gets an improper uniform prior on
(0, ∞). Both of these priors are improper in the sense that there is no way formulate
a density function for them that integrates to 1 over its support.

With cauchy(0,2.5) you limit  the variance. Former gamma-distributions used, but
since studies shown that they could create problems their use is not recommended anymore.

I think the questions refers to that you specify a cauchy but by using a contraint it implies
to become a half-cauchy.

Andre

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am estimating hidden Markov models in Stan that have a special
structure:

1. the transition matrix Theta[K,K] is
  a. small, ie K <= 10,
  b. sparse, with each state transitioning into about K/2 or K/3 states,
  c. has a parametric structure in some parameters x, ie
     Theta[i,j] = some closed form function of x.

I am interested in x mainly, it is about 8-10 parameters.

2. the emission matrix Phi[K,V] has the property that
  a. the number of states V is small, 3 to 5,
  b. each v can come from a small number of k states, and only those.

3. I have about 4-8 consecutive observations for each individual, but
the actual number of observed patterns in the data is << V^4 or V^8.

The manual has a nice writeup of the general case using various
strategies. However, given the structure, I am wondering if there is
something which would be faster. For example, the semi-supervised
algorithm in the manual uses the log likelihood in the accumulator, but
I know a priori that certain likelihoods are 0 because of the sparse &
partitioned structure. Should I somehow take advantage of this? Eg I was
thinking of writing a program (eg in Lisp) that generates Stan code for
each pattern of observations, writes to a Stan file, and uses that
directly.

I know this is very general, but advice would be appreciated, even if it
is along the lines of "try this, it may not work but then you have
learned something" :D

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We are trying to fit this model:

STANDARDIZATION: The covariates x_j were standardized by subtracting the mean in the sample and dividing by country-level standard deviations (this includes areas outside the sample so standard deviations of x_j are not 1 but roughly 0.3). The Cauchy priors are scaled using the population standard deviation in y. This is similar to standardizing the outcome y before fitting the model in Stan.

PARAMETRIZATION: We use the "Matt trick" for tau_q, delta_q, psi_d, theta_j, and alpha_h. See the code.

CONVERGENCE: The model converges according to the all Rhats < 1.05 criterion, but not according to convergence.R <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-dev/_SJBiCaUbt4>. The zip file stan_MVP.zip <https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B8vBpbGknSK2MkFaS0FiUDF3bGM/view> includes files necessary to run the code below:

> library(rstan)
> set_cppo("fast")
> options(mc.cores = 4)
>
> source("dependence.R")
> source("convergence.R")
> model.3 <- stan_model('MVP Model 3e_SM.stan')
> load("outcome_data")
> #fit <- sampling(model.3, data = outcome_data, chains = 6, iter = 1000)
> #save(fit, file = "model.3e")
> load("model.3e")
> fit
> dependence(fit)
> Rhats = as.vector(summary(fit)$summary[,"Rhat"])
> sum(Rhats > 1.05, na.rm = TRUE) # this is 0
> convergence_test(fit, thin = 5, R = 199) # non-convergence?

QUESTIONS: What re-parametrizations should we look at? Should we change the priors (e.g. switch from Cauchy to Half-Normal)? Should we run the chains longer?

Thank you so much,
Shira

> > Hi all,

> > I have been having some issues with implementation of the horseshoe prior in Stan.
> >
> > Using half-cauchy priors for both the local and global scale parameters results in difficult sampling (slow sampling, divergent transitions even with high acceptance rate and low step-size). Re-parameterizations of the cauchy helps but does not resolve this issue.
> >
> > After much exploration of the posterior samples, the issue seems to occur when the global scale parameter approximates 0.  Under this situation, the local scale for the relevant parameters is forced to extreme values far in the tails of the cauchy. Changing the priors on the scale parameters to student_t(3, 0, 1) alleviates the sampling issues, but results in lower shrinkage of less-relevant parameters towards zero.
> >

In particular, I am thinking of using a boundary avoiding prior (such as a gamma(2, _) per BDA) on the global scale parameter to avoid this degenerate case. messages.subject: Pre-STAN QR Factorization to increase speed and efficiency of STAN?
messages.subject_clean: Pre-STAN QR Factorization to increase speed and efficiency of STAN?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I studied the GLM regression algorithms and found this wonderful site
in which Mike Kane and Brian W. Lewis describe some variants to the
ILRS algorithms which use various methods to increase the efficiency
and speed of the GLM regression:

http://bwlewis.github.io/GLM/

Suppose I would do in STAN, considering the QR factorization (only scratch)
    g      = family()$linkinv(t)
    gprime = family()$mu.eta(t)
    z      = t + (b - g) / gprime
    W      = as.vector(gprime^2 / family()$variance(g))
    s_old   = s
    C   = chol(crossprod(Q, W*Q))
    s   = forwardsolve(t(C), crossprod(Q,W*z))
    s   = backsolve(C,s)
    t      = Q %*% s
increment_log_prob(log(t));

I would cut the loop and let the optimization part to STAN. Instead of working at the real data, this algorithm works on the QR
part.

Pre-work done in the transformed data section:

 s = t  = 0
  QR = qr(A)
  Q  = qr.Q(QR)
  R  = qr.R(QR)

What I want to know, before I change the R code into STAN: Is this possible in STAN?
Or does the HḾC struggle with this approach?

Andre

Stan doesn't have any IRLS optimization algorithms. Also, anything where the QR decomposition has to be invoked every time the log-posterior is evaluated is going to be slow because you have to call qr_Q() to get Q and qr_R() to get R. However, we are starting to do some reparameterizations using the QR decomposition (once) in regression models, not because it executes quickly but because it changes the posterior geometry in much the same way that the Matt trick does.

messages.subject: Re: WAIC for (joint) multinomial distribution
messages.subject_clean: WAIC for (joint) multinomial distribution
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, December 8, 2015 at 1:57:10 AM UTC+2, Henrik Singmann wrote:
> Thanks a lot for your response. Unfortunately, I fear that I cannot follow your suggestion of directly using one of the data sets to predict the other one, as in my real model they receive different predictions (as shown below).

If you can compute separate log_lik's as you have done now, then you can do what I suggested :)

WAIC is approximating pointwise predictive performance (or loss). What pointwise means is defined by how you divide the computation of log_lik in generated quantities. In your example here you have n=2 with respect to the asymptotic properties of WAIC. In our paper http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf we show that WAIC does not work so well if n is small (as in here).

>
> My goal is to compare two or more different cognitive models that can generate predictions for the data and select the one that strikes the best balance between model fit and flexibility using WAIC

The best balance is the one giving best predictive performance, so you can just focus on that.

> The models usually have different numbers of parameters and can have quite different functional forms. The example model was a very stripped down version of one such model. In a more realistic case I would have also have a second version of that model that has one parameter or more to predict the difference between the two data sets (k_200 and k_1500; as can be seen from the proportion, there is a sizable difference in the proportion of c responses).

It seems that this additional parameter is very useful. The previous results were likely to be really bad because the fitted parameter could not explain either k_200 or k_1500 and both parts were very influential. In the new model the new parameter helps but now it is likely that WAIC is slightly optimistic (due to reasons discussed in our paper), which may make the model comparison more difficult.

>
> My ultimate goal is to do this in an hierarchical fashion. The current data is aggregated across a huge number of participants ( > 800) such that each participant contributes one multinomial distribution for each condition (k_200 and k_1500) with around 20 data points in each. So overall I have a lot of data. Nevertheless, before attempting the hierarchical version I wanted to know if and how I can actually use WAIC for multinomial data. How do I actually set up the log-likelihoods to get a reasonable value.

You can use WAIC (or even better PSIS-LOO) with multinomial data. And if the data is divisible so that you can compute more than two log_lik's in generated quantieties then things are better. Even then if you hierarchical model is such that each multinomial has it's own parameters and so that p_eff is large compared to n, then WAIC approximation is not accurate (see the above mentioned paper and http://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7461).

Additional benefit of PSIS-LOO is that it gives you khat values, which tells if PSIS-LOO or WAIC is likely to fail. It seems that we (i.e. Jonah) should add similar diagnostic directly to WAIC since people keep using it.

Btw. I once worked with multinomial model for cognitive data, but unfortunately we had lot of zeroes in the data and the results were extremely sensitive to prior. Luckily you seem to have much more data.

Aki

>
> I extended my toy model to be more realistic and actually the estimate of p_waic seems more reasonable. I also added the output of the R code to show the data. I hope this works better for you.
>
> Cheers,
> Henrik
>
> require(rstan)
>
>
> d <- structure(list(db = c(200L, 1500L), bl = c(4460, 3860
> ), r = c(6002, 5350), npl = c(988, 905), c = c(11815,
> 12930)), .Names = c("db", "b", "r", "npl", "c"
> ), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")
> d
> ##     db    b    r npl     c
> ## 1  200 4460 6002 988 11815
> ## 2 1500 3860 5350 905 12930
> prop.table(d[1,-1])
> #           b         r        npl         c
> # 1 0.1917043 0.2579841 0.04246723 0.5078444
> prop.table(d[2,-1])
> #           b         r        npl         c
> # 2 0.1674984 0.2321545 0.03927099 0.5610762
>
>
> m1 <- "
> data {
>   int<lower=1> n_200;
>   int<lower=1> n_1500;
>   int<lower=0> k_200[4];
>   int<lower=0> k_1500[4];
> }
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> c;
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> r;
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> u;
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> c2;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   simplex[4] theta_200;
>   simplex[4] theta_1500;
>
>   theta_200[1] <- c;
>   theta_200[2] <- (1 - c) * r;
>   theta_200[3] <- (1 - c) * (1 - r) * u;
>   theta_200[4] <- (1 - c) * (1 - r) * (1 - u);
>
>   theta_1500[1] <- c2;
>   theta_1500[2] <- (1 - c2) * r;
>   theta_1500[3] <- (1 - c2) * (1 - r) * u;
>   theta_1500[4] <- (1 - c2) * (1 - r) * (1 - u);
> }
> model {
>   // Data
>   k_200 ~ multinomial(theta_200);
>   k_1500 ~ multinomial(theta_1500);
> }
> generated quantities {
>   real log_lik[2];
>
>   log_lik[1] <- multinomial_log(k_200, theta_200);
>   log_lik[2] <- multinomial_log(k_1500, theta_1500);
> }
>
> "
>
> dat <- list(n_200 = sum(d[1,-1]), k_200 = unlist(d[1,c("c", "r", "b", "npl")]),
>             n_1500 = sum(d[2,-1]), k_1500 = unlist(d[2,c("c", "r", "b", "npl")])  )
> ## $n_200
> ## [1] 23265
> ##
> ## $k_200
> ##     c     r     b   npl
> ## 11815  6002  4460   988
> ##
> ## $n_1500
> ## [1] 23045
> ##
> ## $k_1500
> ##     c     r     b   npl
> ## 12930  5350  3860   905
>
>
> samples <- stan(model_code=m1,
>                  data=dat,
>                  iter=1000
> )
>
>
> require(loo)
> waic(extract_log_lik(samples))
> ## Computed from 2000 by 2 log-likelihood matrix
> ##
> ##           Estimate  SE
> ## elpd_waic    -33.2 0.3
> ## p_waic         2.4 0.1
> ## waic          66.4 0.6
>
>
>
>
>
>
> Am Montag, 7. Dezember 2015 21:38:10 UTC+1 schrieb Aki Vehtari:
> > I didn't fully understand your model as the data is obfuscated by R code (I don't understand the lines which create d and dat).
> >
> > The only parameters in your model are simplex[4] theta, so the maximum p is 3. Estimated p_waic is 69.5, so clearly you are doing something which does not work.
> >
> > With the current code having two log_lik components and if you consider WAIC as an asymptotic approximation of leave-one-out cross-validation (which is ok, although it was originally derived as asymptotic approximation of genralisation error directly), then you can think whether you would consider it to be sensible to predict k_1500 given only k_200 and to predict k_200 given only k_1500? If this is sensible then you should do that exactly and not with WAIC approximation which works well only when you have much more observations than parameters. By "exactly" I really mean exactly, and not with PSIS-LOO in loo package. You can use the same code as for the k-fold-CV in our paper related to the loo package. If you would prefer leaving out only one observed value (not all for one multinomial as now), then it's more complicated, but even then WAIC is likely to fail since you don't have much data.
> >
> > And finally: Why do you want to compute WAIC? What is your predictive task, which performance you are assessing?
> >
> > Aki
> >
> > On Monday, December 7, 2015 at 8:35:04 PM UTC+2, Henrik Singmann wrote:
> > > Hello everyone,
> > >
> > > I am trying to implement WAIC for a simple case where the data comes from two multinomial distributions and am hoping to get feedback if my approach is correct. More precisely, WAIC requires the log-likelihood for each data point and sample, but with the inbuilt density function for the multinomial distribution we can only get the log likelihood for the whole multinomial distribution and not for the individual data points. Is it nevertheless appropriate to use WAIC in this case then?
> > > For example, in my case I have two multinomials and then only get two log likelihoods per posterior sample.
> > >
> > > A toy example follows below (using R and the loo package for WAIC).
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > > Henrik
> > >
> > > require(rstan)
> > >
> > > d <- structure(list(db = c(200L, 1500L), bl = c(4460, 3860
> > > ), r = c(6002, 5350), npl = c(988, 905), c = c(11815,
> > > 12930)), .Names = c("db", "b", "r", "npl", "c"
> > > ), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")
> > > d
> > >
> > >
> > > m1 <- "
> > > data {
> > >   int<lower=1> n_200;
> > >   int<lower=1> n_1500;
> > >   int<lower=0> k_200[4];
> > >   int<lower=0> k_1500[4];
> > > }
> > > parameters {
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> c;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> r;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> u;
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >   simplex[4] theta;
> > >
> > >   theta[1] <- c;
> > >   theta[2] <- (1 - c) * r;
> > >   theta[3] <- (1 - c) * (1 - r) * u;
> > >   theta[4] <- (1 - c) * (1 - r) * (1 - u);
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >   // Data
> > >   k_200 ~ multinomial(theta);
> > >   k_1500 ~ multinomial(theta);
> > > }
> > > generated quantities {
> > >   real log_lik[2];
> > >
> > >   log_lik[1] <- multinomial_log(k_200, theta);
> > >   log_lik[2] <- multinomial_log(k_1500, theta);
> > > }
> > >
> > > "
> > >
> > > dat <- list(n_200 = sum(d[1,-1]), k_200 = unlist(d[1,c("c", "r", "b", "npl")]),
> > >             n_1500 = sum(d[2,-1]), k_1500 = unlist(d[2,c("c", "r", "b", "npl")])  )
> > >
> > > samples <- stan(model_code=m1,
> > >                  data=dat,
> > >                  iter=1000
> > > )
> > >
> > > require(loo)
> > > waic(extract_log_lik(samples))
> > > ## Computed from 2000 by 2 log-likelihood matrix
> > > ##
> > > ##           Estimate  SE
> > > ## elpd_waic   -145.9 1.0
> > > ## p_waic        69.5 0.7
> > > ## waic         291.8 2.1
> > >
> > >

  real<lower=0, upper=1> x[5];

bound and you should be good to go.

messages.body_plain:
Check out the manual chapter on user-defined functions and
on variable transforms (there are examples of user defined
densities there).

The basic idea is to define a function to do it

functions {

  real my_density_log(real y, real b, real c, real lb, real ub) {
    compute log density and return
  }

}

and then you can access it using sampling statements.  And you better make
sure that y > 0 everywhere on the interval you care about or the density
won't make sense.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hello Andre,

Are you referring to this post: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/8RerHVzxjUQ ?

That model is wonderful, and you and others are providing great help!

I must confess that I am only casually familiar with VAR and GARCH models, having never used them myself.

That being said, it is my impression that 1) VAR models, although multivariate, don't hold quite the same meaning as the MAR [I can expand my thinking if asked]; 2) GARCH (like ARMA), is univariate, and my interests are specifically in the multivariate case.

Am I correct to understand that your models, wonderful as they are, are not necessarily substitutes for a MAR model? I will, however, be looking at ARMA, GARCH, and VAR examples that I've found to understand some of the relevant coding tricks.

For a model of the form  , where  is an 1 x N matrix,  is a N x N matrix,  are shocks at time  (across all , shocks are temporally-independent), with the shocks at any time step having a multivariate normal distribution with mean 0 and covariance matrix .

Initially I want to hold the off-diagonal elements of B constant at 0, and just fit the diagonals. Same for the covariance matrix for the E. Then I want a fancier model where the off diagonals are parameters to fit, too.
​

My field of study is ecology. This Ecological Monograph by Ives et al shows the applications and interpretations in our field (which I don't think are terribly uncommon or unique): https://paperpile.com/shared/lpCAF7 I'm providing that simply as a reference to my language, in case I'm making any mistakes. And to illustrate my motivation for the MAR, in case that helps point out why I am pursuing MAR instead of something like VAR.

I'll probably get around to writing my own model tomorrow.

-Ryan

> On Dec 10, 2015, at 1:27 PM, Ryan Batt <bat...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> That being said, it is my impression that 1) VAR models, although multivariate, don't hold quite the same meaning as the MAR [I can expand my thinking if asked]; 2) GARCH (like ARMA), is univariate, and my interests are specifically in the multivariate case.
>
> Am I correct to understand that your models, wonderful as they are, are not necessarily substitutes for a MAR model? I will, however, be looking at ARMA, GARCH, and VAR examples that I've found to understand some of the relevant coding tricks.

Wouldn't you be able to extend MAR analogously to the extensions
to AR?

> For a model of the form  , where  is an 1 x N matrix,  is a N x N matrix,  are shocks at time  (across all , shocks are temporally-independent), with the shocks at any time step having a multivariate normal distribution with mean 0 and covariance matrix .

>
> Initially I want to hold the off-diagonal elements of B constant at 0, and just fit the diagonals. Same for the covariance matrix for the E. Then I want a fancier model where the off diagonals are parameters to fit, too.

I'd strongly recommend parameterizing the covariance of the error
distribution using a scaled Cholesky factor for a correlation matrix
with an LKJ prior (see the regression chapter of the manual).

Are you going to try to impose any constraints on B?  And what kind
of prior makes sense?  I saw that it has a stationary distribution if B's
eigenvalues all "live in the unit circle."  We don't usually recommend imposing
such hard constraints (i.e., assuming the process is stationary), but even
if we did, I don't know how we'd code that as a constraint in Stan.  ​

> My field of study is ecology. This Ecological Monograph by Ives et al shows the applications and interpretations in our field (which I don't think are terribly uncommon or unique): https://paperpile.com/shared/lpCAF7 I'm providing that simply as a reference to my language, in case I'm making any mistakes.

Thanks --- that paper's a very nice overview.  We're trying to write
things like that for Stan.  I already did the Dorazio and Royle
occupancy model --- I went through the whole paper and
replicated it with Stan (RStan + knitr, specifically, which works
well for this kind of small-scale coding and presentation):

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/knitr/dorazio-royle-occupancy

It would be fun to take this paper and do the same thing --- replicate it
with Stan code.  We're trying to collect more case studies like the above
from users to distribute as a set of Stan case studies.   We're going to
put them up on our web site.

> And to illustrate my motivation for the MAR, in case that helps point out why I am pursuing MAR instead of something like VAR.
>
> I'll probably get around to writing my own model tomorrow.

Let us know how it goes or you want suggestions for parameterizations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
TLDR: Looks like MAR is what ecologists call VAR. But I still have need to extend the great example provided by Rob Trangucci.

Thanks everyone.

> Ryan,
> ARMA, GARCH can be extended to multidimensional. In case of
> GARCH the co-variance defined as a process over time.
> Shortcut. If you set B entries off diagonal to 0 and same for the innovations (errors),
> then the model could also expressed as independent uni-variate models.
> Andre

Broader context: my motivation for the MAR is to have a multivariate autoregressive component to a more complicated model (a multispecies dynamic occupancy model). With off-diagonals as 0, I think I can still increase model speed by using the matrix multiplication. But your comment here reinforces some other distinctions among these models, and that's helping me along. Thank you!

As for the multivariate extensions, that's what I figured. But I also know that there are a lot of functions in Stan for handling special types of matrices. That, combined with some of the other vocabulary I wasn't familiar with made me think about trying to find a multivariate example before diving in.

> Thanks --- that paper's a very nice overview.  We're trying to write
> things like that for Stan.  I already did the Dorazio and Royle
> occupancy model --- I went through the whole paper and
> replicated it with Stan (RStan + knitr, specifically, which works
> well for this kind of small-scale coding and presentation):
> https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/knitr/dorazio-royle-occupancy <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fstan-dev%2Fexample-models%2Ftree%2Fmaster%2Fknitr%2Fdorazio-royle-occupancy&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNF3cX3P76w5ByG-SCRM1KuGMGN1dw>

The multispecies occupancy model you have there is what I'm extending. I'm extending by 1) adding covariates for occupancy; 2) sites aren't the same; 3) It'll be dynamic, with terms for colonization and extinction (you have a model for that, too, somewhere, but not with some of the other elements).

In some context you might need to make the VAR account for observation error by using a state space representation. I don't think I'll need it in my model, though.

> Are you going to try to impose any constraints on B?  And what kind
> of prior makes sense?  I saw that it has a stationary distribution if B's
> eigenvalues all "live in the unit circle."  We don't usually recommend imposing
> such hard constraints (i.e., assuming the process is stationary), but even
> if we did, I don't know how we'd code that as a constraint in Stan.  ​

The only constraints are that I will initially set the off-diagonals of B to 0. I don't like to code things with the constraint of stationarity, either.

> It would be fun to take this paper and do the same thing --- replicate it
> > with Stan code.  We're trying to collect more case studies like the above
> > from users to distribute as a set of Stan case studies.   We're going to
> > put them up on our web site.

Definitely. That paper has the data online. I know those systems too. I'll also keep in mind that you're looking to make a compendium of those case studies. I can share my stuff as a knitr report like you did.

I fit simulated time series with Rob Trangucci's model. The effective sample size is pretty low; I read in another thread that this seems to happen a lot with time series models. I believe it. Some of the covariance parameters had an Rhat of NaN, which was weird (large ess though). Otherwise the model fit the simulated data pretty well.

What worries me about the ESS is that my occupancy model is super slow, but converges at around 50-100 iterations ... very nice! But I guess that'll disappear once it's dynamic.

Tomorrow I'll extend Rob Trangucci's model to have covariates. I might also put it in a state space representation to hand observation error. I can share that code, if I get working.

Whenever I end up getting the dynamic occupancy model (multispecies, with covariates, non-identical sites) working, I'll share that too. I'll share things using rmarkdown+knitr.

-Ryan

> The other threads about AR models being slow point out that the problems are related to parameterization so making the algebra go faster will not improve the speed of the models.

It doesn't solve the AR-related speed problem. But that's no reason to include slow-downs. It's my understanding that the matrix algebra is a basic increase, regardless of other speed problems. In my case, my multivariate time series can have 400-1000 state variables.

> Priors and the right parameterization might.

Some of the LKJ and Cholesky stuff is tough for me still. Not used to it.  Is there something you'd do differently here: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/8RerHVzxjUQ/iqj6sW3uBQAJ ?

> Also, including colonization and extinction in these models will almost certainly make for poorly identified parameters but I'm add excited as everyone else to see them work.

Yeah, I agree. Right now I'm nervous + excited ... you all know how it goes ;) That said, people have fit models like these before. I'm a little unsure how exactly to implement the model. The models have Psi, the logit of the probability of occupancy, as the target of one of the submodels (the other submodel is Theta, prob of detection). I think I'm going to start by modelling Psi_t = phi * Psi_t-1 +  gamma * (-1 * Psi_t-1) + ..... Where phi is basically the B matrix (AR1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere), Psi is on a logit-scale, and gamma is set up like phi. It's weird because in the JAGS models, you only ever get the phi term OR the gamma term activated, because they model a binary (0,1) latent parameter (Z, occupancy status). Lastly, the .... are the other terms predicting presence/ absence in a vanilla multispecies occupancy model. So maybe the phi and gamma aren't really "persistence" and "colonization" like you might like them to be; they're also not functions of sets of other covariates (but they are species-specific, hierarchically).

You might think I'm crazy, and maybe I am, but I'll give it a try.

> I'm add excited as everyone else to see them work

Yeah, me too!

>
> Non-centering these time series has the potential to drastically
> improve performance, but nonidentifiability is a serious concern,
> especially if the model does not have a strong generative
> interpretation.

Like above, is that VAR model not non-centered? I'll look again late tonight, and tomorrow, but I thought it was when I ran it earlier ... Could you elaborate on your comment about nonidentifiability, and the "strong generative interpretation"? Especially that second statement, but with respect to the first. In the Ives paper he points out how systems with slow return times (large eigen value in the B, I believe; I always get confused by which convention is being used, so maybe it's other way around) are easier to identify. Makes sense. Is that what you mean?

Separate note: what does the "Mark as complete" button mean in Google Groups? I never know if I'm supposed to click it.

I think my basic formulation of the dynamic occupancy model is hugely wrong. So ignore everything I've said there :-/ Marginalizing out the presence-absence parameter is more complicated than simply replacing it with probability of being present, I'm pretty sure.

So when Z is 0 or 1, and you have Psi_t = Z_t-1 * phi + (1 - Z_t-1) * gamma, you can't simply replace Z with Psi and call it a day.
Here's a a paper w/o Z: https://paperpile.com/shared/xlmG6j
Here's a paper w/ Z (in JAGS/ BUGS): https://paperpile.com/shared/EOSUWP

But this is getting pretty off topic from the point of this thread. I might wind up creating a new one.

Stuff about MAR and VAR still fair though.

Sorry.

The models have Psi, the logit of the probability of occupancy, as the target of one of the submodels (the other submodel is Theta, prob of detection). I think I'm going to start by modelling Psi_t = phi * Psi_t-1 +  gamma * (-1 * Psi_t-1) + ..... There are lots of more stable compound functions in Stan like
log_inv_logit and log1m_inv_logit.  Stan does inverse logit

well as speed.

Dear List,

Some Friday fluff for you.

Inspired by the wonderful support in Rstudio, I recently had a quick go at syntax highlighting for Stan via highlight.js <https://github.com/brendan-r/highlightjs_stan> (commonly used for highlighting code in HTML form).

It was a quick lunch-break hack, but it's an improvement on unformatted text, I hope!

I've submitted it as a pull request <https://github.com/isagalaev/highlight.js/pull/1019> to the highlight.js maintainers (it looks like it's being considered for the 9.1 release).

If anyone would like to change/improve it, I'd be very happy to accept a pull request and propagate the changes into the highlight.js PR.

Thanks again for Stan!

Best,

Brendan

messages.body_plain:
(Thought I sent this yesterday, but see now it wasn't)

I found this code:

https://github.com/mclark--/Miscellaneous-R-Code/blob/master/ModelFitting/gp%20Examples/gpStanModelCode.stan

which implements the fitting+prediction using the "Analytical Form of Joint Predictive Inference" approach.

One thing, however, is that since the noise term sigma_sq is added to the diagonal of both Sigma and Omega, I believe the resulting predictions reflect uncertainty on are for future observed data series y, whereas I'd like to reflect only uncertainty on the underlying wiggly function. This previous stan-users post (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/wL-O3SSrcAw/iiDcnIGqt9gJ) implies that I merely need omit addition of sigma_sq to the diagonal of Omega to achieve this, however when I do so I get an error immediately upon sampling saying "Error : Exception thrown at line 104: cholesky_decompose: Cholesky decomposition of m failed". So, JA is definitely the person to ask. If you guys would like to eyeball a couple of options, I'd be happy to submit a highlight.js example PR.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rick,

Which interface to Stan are you using? RStan? Some more comments below.

Jonah

> However, at one point I tried moving the declaration and computation of alpha into the transformed parameters block rather than the model block. It took finishing time to about 20 minutes and memory usage per process to about 1.2GB per process. Why did it do this? What's the difference between declaring and computing alpha in the model block as opposed to the transformed parameters block and why did it cause such a difference in performance?

If you declare something in transformed parameters then it's values will be stored whereas the model block is discarded from memory.

> Lastly, if I remove the wide prior on the intercept, this also causes the model to sample slower by roughly one order of magnitude. Is this because if I don't, it assumes a uniform distribution over the real numbers and thus has a much wider space to explore in sampling? This is just a guess, I'd love for someone to correct me or confirm my suspicion.

Yeah that's right. The default prior is a (potentially improper) uniform on the support of the parameter.

In general we recommend informative or weakly informative priors, rather than the wide priors you currently have. For logistic regression with scaled predictors the coefficients are basically guaranteed to be small (in the -5 to 5 range, roughly), so even something like a normal(0,5) is not a very informative prior. I think Aki recommends a t distribution with 7 df as a default prior for logistic regression coefficients. Of course if you have real prior knowledge you can do even better.

Also for the scale parameters (your sigmas) the constrained uniform can be problematic. We'd recommend a 'soft' constraint via some decaying distribution, like cauchy(0, 2.5) or even tighter, with the parameter declared with lower=0. If you do want to use the uniforms then you should declare sigma with the upper bound you want and then not specify a prior in the model block for it.

I'm having a problem specifying a Wiener drift diffusion model. I'm attempting to specify the boundary separation using an intercept and a coefficient:
