messages.subject: rngs for inference and generated quantities
messages.subject_clean: rngs for inference and generated quantities
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I was wondering if Stan uses a single rng stream for the inference part (anything which is not generated quantities) and the prediction part (the generated quantities part). What makes people often confused is that they change something which only affects the generated quantities part, but this then changes the exact numerical values of the inference part - which happens if a single random number generator stream is used for inference and prediction.

It would be great to use distinct random number streams for inference and prediction such that same model and same data always give the same inference, regardless of the prediction being made. Is that desirable for other users and would it be doable in Stan? If both can be answered with yes, then I am happy to file a feature request...

Cheers,
Sebastian

PS: This may sound like an odd problem, but really, it often confuses our users here.

It was mentioned in the release announcement

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/NEWS

Aside from the longstanding idea of having #include statements in Stan programs, there is nothing in the R implementation that is going to facilitate or inhibit doing it with stanc. The stanc_builder function in R just reads the original Stan program into a R character vector, replaces lines that have things like #include "foo.txt" with the contents of foo.txt, and parses the result with stanc.

If someone wants to use CmdStan to estimate the model, they can still use R (or any scripting language) to construct a .stan file. So, I don't think it is a big priority to implement #include statements in stanc.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Heteroskedasticity and Correlated Errors in Stan
messages.body_plain:
I was curious if anyone has any experience with heteroskedasticity and correlated errors in Stan. Like a GLS approach.

For instance, consider Y generated from the R code below. What approach would be recommended assuming Y and X are known, but sigma and G are not?

I can do simple things like give the regression parameters a multivariate distribution, but I'm not sure if that is really sufficient in the presence of correlated errors. A multivariate normal distribution fit to Y doesn't make sense because if you fit it to cross-sectional data there's only one observation. Perhaps some kind of transformation?

N <- 1000
X <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)
G <- rnorm(N, 1, 0.1)

sigma <- G%*%t(G) + diag(rep(1, N))

Y <- X + rnorm(N, 0, 1) %*% chol(sigma)

Sorry Bob,

I realized I didn't explain the whole picture. c and a are within the data, they are not parameters.

Below you find the model. This LDA model imply that the probability of a word happening in a topic is expressed as linear function where the explanatory variable is (let's say) the humor of a person (this is a parallelism for a bio-informatic problem).

functions {
  real linear_fx_log(real phi, real x, real a, real c) {

    //if(a > 0) return log(c) + log1p((a*x)/c);
    //else return log(c) + log1m((-a*x)/c);
    return (a*x) + c; // THIS LINE //
  }
}
data {
  int<lower=2> K;               // num topics
  int<lower=2> W;               // num words
  int<lower=1> M;               // num docs
  int<lower=1> N;               // total word instances
  int<lower=0> tot_w_count;     //upper value for word counts
  vector<lower=0, upper=tot_w_count>[N] w_count;   // word count per document (e.g., cat in document 1 is present 5 times)
  int<lower=1,upper=W> w[N];    // word n
  int<lower=1,upper=M> doc[N];  // doc ID for word n
  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;     // topic prior

  matrix[K, W] c;  // THIS LINE //
  matrix[K, W] a;  // THIS LINE //
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic dist for doc m
  real phi; //matrix[K,W] phi; // word dist for topic k
  vector<lower=1.0,upper=2.0>[M] x;  // THIS LINE //
}
model {
  for (m in 1:M) {
    theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // prior
    x[m] ~ uniform(1,2); //prior stage  // THIS LINE //
  }
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real gamma[K];
    for (k in 1:K) {
      phi ~ linear_fx(x[doc[n]], a[k,w[n]], c[k,w[n]]);  // THIS LINE //
      gamma[k] <- (log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi));
    }
    if(w_count[n]>0) increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
  }
}

c and a are provided with the data and I know that x[1,2] * a + c > 0 for any c and a that I provide.

So, your suggested constrain

 1 * a + c > 0
 2 * a + c > 0

is true by definition.

Bw.
Stefano

messages.subject_clean: ODE solution when you know dydt, not y
messages.body_plain:
I suspect this is easy, but I don't see the answer in the manual, and I haven't seen it in my searches yet, either.

Say you have a first-order ODE representing, for example, a river's catch basin.  You have measurements of precipitation, and you have measurements of river flow.  You don't have measurements of the water stored in the ground in that catch basin.  Simplistically, you model this with one state variable representing the stored water, and you model the outflow as an exponential; that is, dydt = -lambda * y.

How do you represent that in Stan's ODE solver?  I think precipitation becomes x_r, and y (the output of integrate_ode()) becomes stored water, but I'm totally unclear where dydt (river flow) fits in.

Thanks,

Bill

messages.subject: Very slow sampling for heirarchical multivariate continuous time / stochastic differential model
messages.subject_clean: Very slow sampling for heirarchical multivariate continuous time / stochastic differential model
messages.body_plain:
I've done up an R function to estimate continuous time panel / time series models (as per https://cran.rstudio.com/web/packages/ctsem/index.html) in a heirarchical fashion. I've cholesky'd and vectorized and noncentered everything I could, but am finding sampling very slow, and would really appreciate some feedback on the model, if anyone has some thoughts. There's a fair bit going on, so to try and explain:

nmanifest observed variables Y are observed at multiple time points for each of nsubjects and arranged into an ndatapoints array of vectors of nmanifest length.

each of the ndatapoints Y vectors is distributed according to some intercept vector MANIFESTMEANS, a latent vector eta multiplied by a loading matrix LAMBDA (though here simply diagonal 1's), and some measurement noise, MANIFESTVARchol.

Each of the ndatapoints latent vectors eta (except the first for each subject) is a function of an intercept, discreteCINT, the earlier vector eta(t-1) multiplied by discreteDRIFT, and some sampled perturbation vector (latentError) multiplied by discreteDIFFUSIONchol. All discretePARAMS are in turn a function of dT (the length of time between observations), and continuous time parameter matrices CINT, DRIFT, DIFFUSIONchol.

The continuous time parameter matrices are (when necessary) recovered from transformed versions (e.g. DRIFTlog) that allow unbounded estimation.

These transformed continuous time parameters are stacked into: vector[nparams] indparams[nsubjects]

each row of indparams (each subjects parameters) is then a function of a hypermeans vector + diag_pre_multiply(hypersd,hypercorrchol) multiplied by random vector indparamsnoise[subjecti]

The model, script and data to run via R are attached. Some chains with a few hundred iterations can be found here:
https://www.dropbox.com/s/3fjs8k4vrqks9ln/example_ctStanFit11.rda?dl=0

Is there some way to vectorize sampling for imputedY (I realise the imputation is not appropriate, but have no missing Y in this data anyway) that I am missing (given that MANIFESTVARchol is not always a diagonal matrix) ?

I'm not totally sure how to diagnose the problems here, and would be very happy for any general guidance / links that might be appropriate... I know that sampling is much faster in some chains than for others, though in general seems slow. Am I expecting too much? It took a day or two to sample the above chains for a fairly small problem size - this clearly won't scale, though I'm eager to see how advi goes once it's in rstan.  There were a few divergent iterations, so I guess I also need a higher adapt delta, but that won't help speed.

Cheers for any help!
Charlie

messages.body_plain:
Resurrecting this older thread because I think I can clarify my statement of the problem now.

Fundamentally this is an instance of multivariate regression, but one where you're not observing samples from the multivariate, but their linear transform in combination with condition contrasts. I believe the most direct analogy from the manual would be the example explored by "6.12. Multivariate Priors for Hierarchical Models" with the exception that only one "individual" is observed per "group", so you can't estimate the parameter sigma.

To express my data-generating R code in words and using a concrete example, we observe test scores of a class before and after lunch. We expect that students vary from one another in their overall performance and also vary from one another in the degree to which lunch/time affects their performance, and of course these two sources of variability could correlate. A given student's pre-lunch score is their intercept minus half their lunch effect and their post lunch score is their intercept plus half their lunch effect. Of course, I could simply compute each student's mean score and the difference between pre-lunch/post-lunch scores, and there's my data for the multivariate normal, but I'd have thought that there would be a way to express this model using just the observed test scores. Also, when I have this sorted out, I'm aiming to apply this to a more complicated design where the students are additionally observed on multiple days with some missing data for some students on some days, so direct computation of each subject's intercept & effects isn't possible.

Does this clarification help?

messages.body_plain:
Hey Jonah,

Thanks a ton for the information! I also should have specified that I'm calling Stan through Pystan and not Rstan. Does that make a difference in terms of efficiency?

Regarding the choice of extremely wide priors, you're right and I adjusted them to weakly informative. That massively sped up sampling - I had only chosen them to be that wide arbitrarily and because I was originally adapting the examples from the PyMC3 site. I'm not sure why they chose such broad priors, but going through the Stan reference manual, they do repeatedly suggest informative or weakly informative priors.

Thanks for the tip on using the cauchy instead of the constrained uniform - I didn't realize that was problematic.

This is a lot clearer now and I've been able to keep my memory usage to a reasonable amount now that I know what causes variables to be stored and what doesn't!

Thanks again,
Rick

El domingo, 13 de diciembre de 2015, 15:09:15 (UTC-8), Jonah Gabry escribió:
> Hi Rick,
>
> Which interface to Stan are you using? RStan? Some more comments below.
>
> Jonah
>
>
> > However, at one point I tried moving the declaration and computation of alpha into the transformed parameters block rather than the model block. It took finishing time to about 20 minutes and memory usage per process to about 1.2GB per process. Why did it do this? What's the difference between declaring and computing alpha in the model block as opposed to the transformed parameters block and why did it cause such a difference in performance?
>
> If you declare something in transformed parameters then it's values will be stored whereas the model block is discarded from memory.
>
> > Lastly, if I remove the wide prior on the intercept, this also causes the model to sample slower by roughly one order of magnitude. Is this because if I don't, it assumes a uniform distribution over the real numbers and thus has a much wider space to explore in sampling? This is just a guess, I'd love for someone to correct me or confirm my suspicion.
>
> Yeah that's right. The default prior is a (potentially improper) uniform on the support of the parameter.
>
> In general we recommend informative or weakly informative priors, rather than the wide priors you currently have. For logistic regression with scaled predictors the coefficients are basically guaranteed to be small (in the -5 to 5 range, roughly), so even something like a normal(0,5) is not a very informative prior. I think Aki recommends a t distribution with 7 df as a default prior for logistic regression coefficients. Of course if you have real prior knowledge you can do even better.
>
> Also for the scale parameters (your sigmas) the constrained uniform can be problematic. We'd recommend a 'soft' constraint via some decaying distribution, like cauchy(0, 2.5) or even tighter, with the parameter declared with lower=0. If you do want to use the uniforms then you should declare sigma with the upper bound you want and then not specify a prior in the model block for it.
>

Yeah, those really wide priors used to be the state of the art, and they are still pretty common. Thanks, Daniel,

we normally use the Bayesian versions of nonmem to model pharmakokinetic data, but it also has problems with unknown injection times - with the exception of one overall delay that can be easily modelled.

With the real data, we know that the injection time is 100 and 400 seconds, but from the data one can easily see that there is a transport-lag (not a diffusion lag) of between 10 and 20 seconds, and additional lags between tissues.

For a first look at the data, I tried a simplified analysis by fitting overlapping exponentials with prior-constrained onset; no ode or other differential equations involved, code exaclty as given. In the simulated example, I put a prior on the lag and tried to estimate it.

However, this brings Stan to a crawl, and I was not sure estimating a parameter with a discontinuity is a valid approach at all.

Dieter

messages.subject: Modeling binary, longitudinal data with missing values
messages.subject_clean: Modeling binary, longitudinal data with missing values
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for Stan, so very useful and powerful.

I have binary outcomes for a large number of items (I1-I3 in example below) over a number of time-ordered sessions (S1-S4 below). For each session there is only partial information, i.e. outcomes for some items are missing. In typical use cases the number of items are in the thousands and the number of items are in the range 50-1000.

Example:

Item,S1,S2,S3,S4
I1,0,1,X,0
I2,1,1,0,0
I3,X,0,0,0

For each item I want to predict the probability of getting an outcome of 1 in the next session. It is reasonable to assume there is both long-term and short-term trends, i.e. items that have had many 1's overall are more likely to have 1 in next session, and items that recently had many 1's is more likely to have a 1 in next session. It is also reasonable to assume that the items are clustered/grouped where items in a cluster/group behave similarly. This clustering can, at least as a first approximation, be assumed to be static, i.e. not change over time.

I have been thinking of some kind of logistic regression combined with ARIMA combined with some indian/chinese buffet process for the clustering but I'd appreciate pointers to papers/models or even Stan code that is relevant for my case.

Thanks in advance, Robert Feldt

messages.subject_clean: PSIS-LOO for trial-by-trial modeling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan,

I've been modeling a 2-armed bandit task with a basic reinforcement learning model in a trial-by-trial fashion. For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.

When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.

(1) I wonder if I am doing this correctly? Is the model comparison based on PSIS-LOO still reliable?
(2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Am I suppose run a k(-trial)-fold CV per subject, or run a k(-subject)-fold CV for all the subjects? Any suggestions about how to calculate a k-fold CV for such a reinforcement learning model?
(3) or alternatively, how about using WAIC?

You may want to check the attached stan model file. Any input/suggestion is welcome.

> loo_RL
Computed from 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix

         Estimate    SE
elpd_loo  -6920.1 150.0
p_loo       172.6  13.0
looic     13840.2 299.9
Warning messages:
1: 110 (85.3%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
2: 19 (14.7%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1

> loo_RLnc
Computed from 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix

         Estimate    SE
elpd_loo  -6562.5 166.6
p_loo       230.7   8.9
looic     13125.1 333.2
Warning messages:
1: 74 (57.4%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
2: 55 (42.6%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1

> compare(loo_RL, loo_RLnc)
elpd_diff        se   weight1   weight2
    357.6      42.3       0.0       1.0

Thanks in advance!

Lei

On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:22:59 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> Hi Stan,
>

For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.

It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.

>
> When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.
>
> (1) I wonder if I am doing this correctly? Is the model comparison based on PSIS-LOO still reliable?

Based on a quick look, it seems your code is correct. Large khats tell that PSIS-LOO is not reliable. PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.

> (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Am I suppose run a k(-trial)-fold CV per subject, or run a k(-subject)-fold CV for all the subjects? Any suggestions about how to calculate a k-fold CV for such a reinforcement learning model?

I recommend k-fold-CV where data is divided based on subjects (e.g. with k=10, leave 12-13 subjects out in each fold). Vehtari et al (2015) has an example code. If you are able to compute separate log_lik for each subject (summing 100 trials) as in your current code, then you can do the same also for the test data in k-fold-CV. We could add some helper functions to make the data divisions to training and test sets (I have them in Matlab, but need to port to R and Python, too).

> (3) or alternatively, how about using WAIC?

If PSIS-LOO fails then WAIC fails, too. Currently our WAIC code just doesn't warn you about that. Adding warnings to our WAIC code is on TODO list.

Aki

Hi!

Apologies for going stray slightly, but this happens so often: Suppose I want to do k-fold-cv on the basis of subjects as in the example described by Lei - in his case I understood that each subject has exactly 100 trials. However, I am often facing the situation that subjects can have vastly different number of observations. Is a leave-subjects-out approach then meaningful or should on average each subject have the same number of observations?

These regular data-sets happen so rarely in my applications...

Thanks (Aki)!

Sebastian

On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:21:30 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:

>
>
> On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:22:59 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> > Hi Stan,
> >
> > I've been modeling a 2-armed bandit task with a basic reinforcement learning model in a trial-by-trial fashion. For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.
>
> It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.
>
> >
> > When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.
> >
> > (1) I wonder if I am doing this correctly? Is the model comparison based on PSIS-LOO still reliable?
>
> Based on a quick look, it seems your code is correct. Large khats tell that PSIS-LOO is not reliable. PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.
>
>
> > (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Am I suppose run a k(-trial)-fold CV per subject, or run a k(-subject)-fold CV for all the subjects? Any suggestions about how to calculate a k-fold CV for such a reinforcement learning model?
>

> Aki

On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 6:23:39 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:

>
> (1) partition data. If I would run a 10-fold-CV, leading to 12-13 subjects per fold. Do I randomly select subjects per fold, or systematically? Do I only run model fitting K times, or with M different data partition method and fit the model M x K times?

If the subjects are exchangeable that is the order does not contain information then there is no need for random selection. If the order does contain information, e.g. in survival studies the later patients have shorter follow-up, then randomization is often useful. I would randomly permute the subjects and then systemically divide them to 10 groups. I would do only one random permutation and systematic division and run model fitting 10 times. Making several permutations can reduce variance, but the effect is usually negligible for stable inference. Other approaches for selecting subjects randomly have higher variance than the procedure I suggested above. In some cases it may be useful to use stratification to get more balanced groups.

> (2) obtaining the k-fold-cv output. Suppose I run a 10-fold-cv with systematically selecting subjects (i.e. first 13, second 13, and so on...), and I obtain ten log-likelihood matrix, one for each testing fold. What to do next to summarize the results and compare different models?
> As I understood the paper, once I get 10 loglik matrix, e.g. for a single 4000-by-13 loglik matrix L, I sum L across the time of simulations S and divide the results by S: rowSum(L)/S; then I sum such results across the 10 folds. This is then the k-fold-cv result for model comparison. Am I correct here?

I would compute loglik for each subject and combine the results from different runs to get 4000-by-129 loglik matrix as in LOO. Instead of loo function you can compute elpd_loo as sum(log(mean(exp(log_lik)))), where mean is along the draws and sum along the subjects. You can use pointwise contributions (before the sum) as in LOO. Maybe we should make a helper function, which would create from k-fold-cv log_liks a object which could be given to compare function. I have examples in Matlab, but unfortunately I'm still learning R.

On Saturday, December 19, 2015 at 12:09:16 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:

Could I still derive p_loo using the variance-based calculation from the 4000-by-129 loglik matrix? If so, that will be really great.

Do you really need an estimate of the effective number of parameters? Some bias correction terms in information criterion literature have been called as effective number of parameters, but 1) you don't need that because you already have the predictive performance estimate, 2) interpretation of the bias correction or difference between lpd and elpd as the effective is not clear (e.g. in 8 schools example p_waic is allways <= 4, although there is 9 parameters in the model, and difference between lpd and elpd can be >9). You can still compute the difference between lpd and elpd_kfcv and use it as some measure of difference between within-sample and out-of-sample performance, but interpreting it as the effective number of parameters is tricky.

>
> BTW, would you mind sharing your matlab code for k-fold-cv as you mentioned? Is it one of your .m file on your GitHub repository?

You can find it one part of that in GPstuff https://github.com/gpstuff-dev/gpstuff/blob/master/misc/cvit.m
I can add in next few days a full example with Stan to PSIS repo or somewhere...

Aki

> > > Thanks Aki, for your clear and comprehensive comment and suggestion! I now have two more questions concerning implementing the K-fold-CV. I apologize if those questions seem too naive.
> > >
> > > (1) partition data. If I would run a 10-fold-CV, leading to 12-13 subjects per fold. Do I randomly select subjects per fold, or systematically? Do I only run model fitting K times, or with M different data partition method and fit the model M x K times?
> >
> > If the subjects are exchangeable that is the order does not contain information then there is no need for random selection. If the order does contain information, e.g. in survival studies the later patients have shorter follow-up, then randomization is often useful. I would randomly permute the subjects and then systemically divide them to 10 groups. I would do only one random permutation and systematic division and run model fitting 10 times. Making several permutations can reduce variance, but the effect is usually negligible for stable inference. Other approaches for selecting subjects randomly have higher variance than the procedure I suggested above. In some cases it may be useful to use stratification to get more balanced groups.
> >
> >
> > > (2) obtaining the k-fold-cv output. Suppose I run a 10-fold-cv with systematically selecting subjects (i.e. first 13, second 13, and so on...), and I obtain ten log-likelihood matrix, one for each testing fold. What to do next to summarize the results and compare different models?
> > > As I understood the paper, once I get 10 loglik matrix, e.g. for a single 4000-by-13 loglik matrix L, I sum L across the time of simulations S and divide the results by S: rowSum(L)/S; then I sum such results across the 10 folds. This is then the k-fold-cv result for model comparison. Am I correct here?
> >
> > I would compute loglik for each subject and combine the results from different runs to get 4000-by-129 loglik matrix as in LOO. Instead of loo function you can compute elpd_loo as sum(log(mean(exp(log_lik)))), where mean is along the draws and sum along the subjects. You can use pointwise contributions (before the sum) as in LOO. Maybe we should make a helper function, which would create from k-fold-cv log_liks a object which could be given to compare function. I have examples in Matlab, but unfortunately I'm still learning R.
> >
> >
> > > And does it also make sense to multiply it with -2 to translate it on the information criterion scale?
> > >
> >

> > > > > Hi Stan,

> > > > > I've been modeling a 2-armed bandit task with a basic reinforcement learning model in a trial-by-trial fashion. For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.
> > > >
> > > > It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.
> > > > >

> > > >
> > > > Based on a quick look, it seems your code is correct. Large khats tell that PSIS-LOO is not reliable. PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Not sure why you took the LKJ prior parameter
to be the number of inputs.

And you want to use the Cholesky-factor parameterization.

messages.body_plain:
We're about to release a stiff ode solver, which will hopefully help
mitigate some of the freezing problems we currently have with the ODE
solver.  No guarantee that it's going to be faster, but it should be much
more robust to outliers.

- Bob

> On Dec 17, 2015, at 12:39 PM, Dieter Menne <menne...@googlemail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> Thanks, Daniel,
>
> we normally use the Bayesian versions of nonmem to model pharmakokinetic data, but it also has problems with unknown injection times - with the exception of one overall delay that can be easily modelled.
>
> With the real data, we know that the injection time is 100 and 400 seconds, but from the data one can easily see that there is a transport-lag (not a diffusion lag) of between 10 and 20 seconds, and additional lags between tissues.
>
> For a first look at the data, I tried a simplified analysis by fitting overlapping exponentials with prior-constrained onset; no ode or other differential equations involved, code exaclty as given. In the simulated example, I put a prior on the lag and tried to estimate it.

> However, this brings Stan to a crawl, and I was not sure estimating a parameter with a discontinuity is a valid approach at all.
>
> Dieter

I'm not exactly an ODE expert, but I don't see how you can
do anything with just dy/dt if you never observe any y (or
derived quantities based on it) and have no constraints on
what it can be to start in the initial conditions.

My electricity and magnetism is still back in the physics
undergrad class I never understood, so that doesn't help me.

- Bob

You're right, of course.  I was thinking / hoping that I could infer when the stored water / charge was 0 by observing when the outflow (river flow or current through the resistor) was 0, giving me y(To), not y(0), but I realize that it's hard to measure accurately when the flow goes to 0 (the slope of the stored water / charge over time is pretty shallow when the stock approaches 0).

So I'm looking at hydrology examples using other packages now (actually, I've been sidetracked onto something else temporarily, but that's what I'm planning).

Still, I wonder if I'm slow or the problem still exists.  What if I have a general ODE problem with inflows and outflows, and I know sufficient initial or boundary conditions?  On top of the initial or boundary conditions on y (e.g., the value of y at some point To), I know dydt vs. t, not y vs. t.  I think I can model and solve that in MCSim, since the entire ODE model is in the main MCSim code (actually in the Dynamics {} block), but the ODE mechanics in Stan seems localized to a function with predefined signature.

I was going to try that in MCSim before posting this, but I may not get back to this problem in the next day or three.  Still, it seems like a reasonable PBPK problem: it's cheap to measure when you give drugs and how much you give, but it's costly (in dollars and perhaps pain) to measure concentrations in plasma or other locations.  Are there example PBPK problems done in Stan to review?

Bill

There are multiple problems with your model in this
one line:

>       beta[k] ~ normal(c[k] + a[k] * sigma[m], 0.0001);

you have constrained sigma[m] in (1, 2), but c[k] and a[k]
are unconstrained.  So c[k] + a[k] * sigma[m] is unconstrained.

I'm not sure if you realized that Stan's normal distribution
is parameterized with scale (or standard deviation), not with
precision (1 / std_dev^2).  So the above means you're constraining
beta[k] to be very very close to c[k] + a[k] * sigma[m].

- Bob

one line:

>       beta[k] ~ normal(c[k] + a[k] * sigma[m], 0.0001);

you have constrained sigma[m] in (1, 2), but c[k] and a[k]
are unconstrained.

in Stan.  And that also should hold for MCSim, as well.  The problem
here is that at no point have you completely specified your ODE system,
parameters, and data.  We speculated a bit on your initial partial
information, but if that speculation wasn’t sufficient then you’ll have to
provide the complete system.

I was thinking / hoping that I could infer when the stored water / charge was 0 by observing when the outflow (river flow or current through the resistor) was 0, giving me y(To), not y(0), but I realize that it's hard to measure accurately when the flow goes to 0 (the slope of the stored water / charge over time is pretty shallow when the stock approaches 0).
>
> So I'm looking at hydrology examples using other packages now (actually, I've been sidetracked onto something else temporarily, but that's what I'm planning).
>
> Still, I wonder if I'm slow or the problem still exists.  What if I have a general ODE problem with inflows and outflows, and I know sufficient initial or boundary conditions?  On top of the initial or boundary conditions on y (e.g., the value of y at some point To), I know dydt vs. t, not y vs. t.  I think I can model and solve that in MCSim, since the entire ODE model is in the main MCSim code (actually in the Dynamics {} block), but the ODE mechanics in Stan seems localized to a function with predefined signature.
>
> I was going to try that in MCSim before posting this, but I may not get back to this problem in the next day or three.  Still, it seems like a reasonable PBPK problem: it's cheap to measure when you give drugs and how much you give, but it's costly (in dollars and perhaps pain) to measure concentrations in plasma or other locations.  Are there example PBPK problems done in Stan to review?

Well, since I am on development stage I though: since beta is going all over the places (Infinite) when it should stay well close to my linear regression, I will give SD a really low value so it will "stick" to the interval 4-6, in the case that I give a=c=2 and sigma (1,2).

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood

is a modification of the LDA likelywood present in the Stan manual https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/download/v2.4.0/stan-reference-2.4.0.pdf

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma)); // likelihood

It has been modified for speed purpose. Because since I have a high number of words (genes ~ 10K gene copies) repetition per document (sample), looping for every word like in the original Stan LDA was a waste of cycles, instead I multiply the probability of one instance (prob of a word in a topic/document) by the copy of that instance.

> conditional print statements.

I will. Anyway for records I explain briefly my model and where I am coming from.

As done before and working for me with Stan, I am applying a LDA model (taken from Stan reference manual https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/download/v2.4.0/stan-reference-2.4.0.pdf) with phi known

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-C1SI48UDLTM/VnewBLowPGI/AAAAAAAAENQ/v_5Lih3HYtc/s1600/lda.png>

data {
  int<lower=2> K;               // num topics
  int<lower=2> W;               // num words
  int<lower=1> M;               // num docs
  int<lower=1> N;               // total word instances
  int<lower=0> tot_w_count;     //upper value for word counts
  vector<lower=0, upper=tot_w_count>[N] w_count;   // word count per document (e.g., cat in document 1 is present 5 times)
  int<lower=1,upper=W> w[N];    // word n
  int<lower=1,upper=M> doc[N];  // doc ID for word n
  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;     // topic prior

  simplex[W] phi[K];            // word dist for topic k

}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic dist for doc m
}

model {
  for (m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // prior

  for (n in 1:N) {
    real gamma[K];

    for (k in 1:K) gamma[k] <- (log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]));

    if(w_count[n]>0) increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
  }
}

The modification I am trying to work is: if a topic uses different words depending (linear relationship) on the "mood" (sigma) of the writer (one mood per document), how can I identify sigma (mood) and theta (topic proportion per document)?

Again the information I have is all linear relationships [K, W] (instead of having phi). So instead of having one phi, I will have one phi per document. This phi while provided before, now will be a parameter.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-gHIT98OjRyM/VnewHbETQOI/AAAAAAAAENY/YIwl1VzRJI0/s1600/ldaCA.png>

data {
  int<lower=2> K;               // num topics
  int<lower=2> W;               // num words
  int<lower=1> M;               // num docs
  int<lower=1> N;               // total word instances
  int<lower=0> tot_w_count;     //upper value for word counts
  vector<lower=0, upper=tot_w_count>[N] w_count;   // word count per document (e.g., cat in document 1 is present 5 times)
  int<lower=1,upper=W> w[N];    // word n
  int<lower=1,upper=M> doc[N];  // doc ID for word n
  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;     // topic prior

  real<lower=0> beta_max; //max value for beta based on my data

  matrix[K, W] c;
  matrix[K, W] a;
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic dist for doc m

  real<lower=0, upper=beta_max> beta[M,K,W];     // words prior
  real<lower=0, upper=1> phi[M,K,W];

  vector<lower=1,upper=2>[M] sigma; //mood
}
model {
  for (m in 1:M) {
    theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // prior
    for(k in 1:K) {

      beta[m,k] ~ normal(c[k] + a[k] * sigma[m], 0.0001);
      phi[m,k] ~ dirichlet(to_vector(beta[m,k]));

    }
  }
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real gamma[K];
    for (k in 1:K) gamma[k] <- log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[doc[n],k, w[n]]);
    if(w_count[n]>0) increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
  }
}

Thanks

>
> - Bob

Thanks again Aki. I agree that it becomes tricky when interpreting the estimated effective number of parameters. However, when reporting LOO, PSIS-LOO, or kfcv, given the fact that they are rather new methods for model comparison, I wonder if it is plausible to maintain the results from AIC, BIC, DIC etc. For such consistency reason, I might put the bias correction alongside.

Any comments on the above point, Aki? and other experts opinion?

Last but not least, thanks (Aki) for putting effort on the matlab code. This will be a great contribution to the community.

Best,
Lei

On Saturday, December 19, 2015 at 6:44:38 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> On Saturday, December 19, 2015 at 12:09:16 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> > Thanks again Aki, your explanation is indeed helpful!
> >
> > Just only one more concern: by computing the elpd_loo as you commented, is there also a way to calculate the estimated effective number of parameters 'p_loo' as in the loo()  function? Could I still derive p_loo using the variance-based calculation from the 4000-by-129 loglik matrix? If so, that will be really great.
>
> Do you really need an estimate of the effective number of parameters? Some bias correction terms in information criterion literature have been called as effective number of parameters, but 1) you don't need that because you already have the predictive performance estimate, 2) interpretation of the bias correction or difference between lpd and elpd as the effective is not clear (e.g. in 8 schools example p_waic is allways <= 4, although there is 9 parameters in the model, and difference between lpd and elpd can be >9). You can still compute the difference between lpd and elpd_kfcv and use it as some measure of difference between within-sample and out-of-sample performance, but interpreting it as the effective number of parameters is tricky.
>
> >
> > BTW, would you mind sharing your matlab code for k-fold-cv as you mentioned? Is it one of your .m file on your GitHub repository?
>
> You can find it one part of that in GPstuff https://github.com/gpstuff-dev/gpstuff/blob/master/misc/cvit.m
> I can add in next few days a full example with Stan to PSIS repo or somewhere...
>
> Aki
>
> >
> > Many thanks.
> > Lei
> >
> >
> >

> > On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 7:22:34 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> > >
> > > On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 6:23:39 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> > > > Thanks Aki, for your clear and comprehensive comment and suggestion! I now have two more questions concerning implementing the K-fold-CV. I apologize if those questions seem too naive.
> > > >
> > > > (1) partition data. If I would run a 10-fold-CV, leading to 12-13 subjects per fold. Do I randomly select subjects per fold, or systematically? Do I only run model fitting K times, or with M different data partition method and fit the model M x K times?
> > >
> > > If the subjects are exchangeable that is the order does not contain information then there is no need for random selection. If the order does contain information, e.g. in survival studies the later patients have shorter follow-up, then randomization is often useful. I would randomly permute the subjects and then systemically divide them to 10 groups. I would do only one random permutation and systematic division and run model fitting 10 times. Making several permutations can reduce variance, but the effect is usually negligible for stable inference. Other approaches for selecting subjects randomly have higher variance than the procedure I suggested above. In some cases it may be useful to use stratification to get more balanced groups.
> > >
> > >
> > > > (2) obtaining the k-fold-cv output. Suppose I run a 10-fold-cv with systematically selecting subjects (i.e. first 13, second 13, and so on...), and I obtain ten log-likelihood matrix, one for each testing fold. What to do next to summarize the results and compare different models?
> > > > As I understood the paper, once I get 10 loglik matrix, e.g. for a single 4000-by-13 loglik matrix L, I sum L across the time of simulations S and divide the results by S: rowSum(L)/S; then I sum such results across the 10 folds. This is then the k-fold-cv result for model comparison. Am I correct here?
> > >
> > > I would compute loglik for each subject and combine the results from different runs to get 4000-by-129 loglik matrix as in LOO. Instead of loo function you can compute elpd_loo as sum(log(mean(exp(log_lik)))), where mean is along the draws and sum along the subjects. You can use pointwise contributions (before the sum) as in LOO. Maybe we should make a helper function, which would create from k-fold-cv log_liks a object which could be given to compare function. I have examples in Matlab, but unfortunately I'm still learning R.
> > >
> > >
> > > > And does it also make sense to multiply it with -2 to translate it on the information criterion scale?
> > > >
> > >
> > > I hate multiplying by -2. Without it difference between lpd and elpd_loo is related to the effective number of parameters. I also prefer that larger value is better.
> > >
> > > Aki
> > >
> > > > many thanks again!
> > > > Lei
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:21:30 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:22:59 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> > > > > > Hi Stan,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I've been modeling a 2-armed bandit task with a basic reinforcement learning model in a trial-by-trial fashion. For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.
> > > > >
> > > > > It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (1) I wonder if I am doing this correctly? Is the model comparison based on PSIS-LOO still reliable?
> > > > >
> > > > > Based on a quick look, it seems your code is correct. Large khats tell that PSIS-LOO is not reliable. PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > > (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Am I suppose run a k(-trial)-fold CV per subject, or run a k(-subject)-fold CV for all the subjects? Any suggestions about how to calculate a k-fold CV for such a reinforcement learning model?
> > > > >
> > > > > I recommend k-fold-CV where data is divided based on subjects (e.g. with k=10, leave 12-13 subjects out in each fold). Vehtari et al (2015) has an example code. If you are able to compute separate log_lik for each subject (summing 100 trials) as in your current code, then you can do the same also for the test data in k-fold-CV. We could add some helper functions to make the data divisions to training and test sets (I have them in Matlab, but need to port to R and Python, too).
> > > > >
> > > > > > (3) or alternatively, how about using WAIC?
> > > > >
> > > > > If PSIS-LOO fails then WAIC fails, too. Currently our WAIC code just doesn't warn you about that. Adding warnings to our WAIC code is on TODO list.
> > > > >
> > > > > Aki
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You may want to check the attached stan model file. Any input/suggestion is welcome.

> > > > > > Warning messages:
> > > > > > 1: 110 (85.3%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
> > > > > > 2: 19 (14.7%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1

On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 1:22:34 PM UTC-5, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> I hate multiplying by -2. Without it difference between lpd and elpd_loo is related to the effective number of parameters. I also prefer that larger value is better.
>
> Aki

To be fair, the difference is still directly proportional to the effective number of parameters, just multiplied by -2. If I recall correctly, the -2 comes from the linear regression world where the residual sum of squares (or its log, I forget) is twice the negative loglikihood and is thus related to the deviance and approximately chi square. Burnham and Anderson discuss it in passing in one of their web papers on AIC myths, but atcual text on the original reason for the -2 is admittedly hard to pin down.

Avi

On Monday, December 21, 2015 at 4:00:00 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:

However, when reporting LOO, PSIS-LOO, or kfcv, given the fact that they are rather new methods for model comparison, I wonder if it is plausible to maintain the results from AIC, BIC, DIC etc. For such consistency reason, I might put the bias correction alongside.

If it is tricky, maybe it should not then be reported by default. I'm worried that people over-interpret the meaning of effective number of parameters (as they have been doing for years). It can be useful getting some insight to the complexity of the model (or problems in computation).

Oldest references to cross-validation are before AIC, and Bayesian LOO and kfcv were proposed by Geisser in 1975, so LOO and kfcv are rather old. IS-LOO is from 1992, and only new method is PSIS-LOO, which is just more reliable and accurate way to compute IS-LOO estimates. BIC computes something completely different and should not be listed with other ICs. If you are using Bayesian models, then you should also forget AIC and DIC.

messages.subject: Trying to break Stan's limitations on not using parameters for time in the ODE solver?
messages.subject_clean: Trying to break Stan's limitations on not using parameters for time in the ODE solver?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This may be tilting at windmills, but I'm trying to figure out if there is a way to have an uncertain start time for my ODE; if I'm unsure when an epidemic starts, I'd like to be able to model that, and find the best fit for a dataset for the start time, as well as other parameters. (I didn't see anything about this in the forum history.)

In Stan, the t0 and t inputs into integrate_ODE are fixed; is there any clever way to get around this? (If so, how bad an idea is it to do?)

The obvious idea is to have the start values be smaller, but I think there is an effective lower bound on how few infections I can start with. (That is, 1e-25 doesn't make the sampler happy, and specifying a prior on it is kind of nasty.) Also, this doesn't capture the dynamics well; it ramps up over time, instead of starting above 1 when the infection is imported/emerges.

Thanks for any help, or potential workarounds,
David

messages.subject: Eigenvalue decomposition of covariance matrix
messages.subject_clean: Eigenvalue decomposition of covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Suppose I have several multivariate Gaussians x_i ~ N(0, Sigma_i) but all the Sigma_i are weighted sums of a base covariance K and some noise:

Sigma_i = alpha_i K + eps_i I

K is also probably low rank. This setting lends itself to an eigendecomposition of K=QVQ' (Q orthogonal, V diagonal) from which the inverses of all the Sigma_i can be easily calculated:

Sigma_i^-1 = Q(alpha_i V + eps_i I)Q'

I know I can call eigenvalues_sym and eigenvectors_sym to calculate Q and V but will this do the calculation twice? There does not seem to be any support for sharing the results between calls.

Also is there any way to take advantage of the low rank of K (perhaps by doing a partial eigendecomposition)?

Thanks,
John.

P.S. I think I will see some readers of this list in Lenzerheide so I'm looking forward to that one.

possible.

messages.body_plain:
I don't know what you are suggesting, exactly.

The differential equation system does not use t; I would need to change the offset outside of the ODE system solver. If I offset by a non-multiple of the values to solve at, I need to either adjust the times at which to solve, or use some rough linear kludge, or slow method, to infer the values at the locations I actually need.

As a simple example, how would I do this with Michael Betancourt's compartmental SIR+B model, attached - let's say I know that the bacteria in the y0 were introduced at some point, but I don't know when.

Cheers,
David

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trying to break Stan's limitations on not using parameters for time in the ODE solver?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Trying to break Stan's limitations on not using parameters for time in the ODE solver?
messages.body_plain:
1.  Declare a parameter for the initial time.

2.  Pass that parameter to ode_integrate

3.  Pass initial time t0 = 0 to ode_integrate.

4.  Within the system function (first argument to ode_integrate),
pull out the parameter passed to ode_integrate, assign it to
a local varaible t_delta, then add t_delta to the time argument
in the system.

That parameter t_delta will then be the time offset.  I have
no idea whether this will fit well, but it's the only way I know
how to do this.

I'll try to come up with a working example and add a description
to the next manual release:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1709#issuecomment-166691708

If you get it to work before then, please add a comment to the above
issue.

- Bob

messages.subject: Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis
messages.subject_clean: Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,
I'm pretty new to Stan, and I've been going through the documentation to figure out how to code up a longitudinal factor analysis where the number of time points differs from individual to individual, and the points are unequally spaced. Suppose for example we have two people, the first of whom has two observations, and the second of whom has three. Also suppose that we have 5 outcomes and two factors for each observation. There are two issues I'm not entirely sure how to deal with. Letting i index people, j index time points, k index the outcomes, and p index the factors, (my outcomes are a mix of binaries and counts, so I have to define a custom probability function)

The first is that I'm not sure what is the most reasonable way to declare the outcomes y_ijk and factors f_ijp. I was thinking about defining a single array/vector for all the outcomes using code from the documentation

data {
int<lower=0> N; // # people
int s[J]; // number of records per person
int<lower=0> K; // # of outcomes
int<lower=0> P; // # of factors
vector[N*sum(s)] y; // observations (i don't think this syntax is correct, but hopefully it's clear what I'm trying to accomplish with this)

where y would just be a column vector that looks like

y_111
y_112
.
.
.
y_234
y_235

and then just segment it twice, once to take out all the observations for person 1, and then another time to get the observations for person 1 at time j

model{
  int pos.person;
  int pos.time;
  pos.person <- 1;
  for(i in 1:N){
    pos.time <- 1;
    for(j in 1:s[i]){
      ysub <- segment(segment(y,pos.person,s[i]*K),pos.time,pos.time+K-1) // Vector containing the jth measurement for person i
      increment_log_prob(X) // X is going to be a custom probability function for the entries of ysub which involves the factors and factor loadings
      pos.time <- pos.time + K
    }
    pos.person <- pos.person + s[i]*K
  }
}

I don't think the syntax is completely correct, but the basic idea is just taking all of the outcomes for all of the individuals at all of the time points, stacking them, and then just defining the density on subsets of that vector as per page 145 of the documentation.

I know that if my data were really this simple that I could just define vectors y_11 up to y_23, but my actual data has upwards of 10,000 records and 100 outcomes which is why I'm trying to find another way to do this. So my overall question has 3 parts. 1) Does the above idea for doing this even work at all? 2) If it does work, can I also do this for the factors, i.e. define a gigantic vector of factors and then in the model just specify multivariate normal priors on segments of the vector? 3) If this does work, is there a more efficient way to handle this issue?

My only other issue is that to define the multivariate normal distributions for the factors, I am using gaussian processes to handle the unequal time spacing, and I would like to make use of Kronecker products, but I get the impression that hasn't yet been implemented in Stan. Is defining it element-wise still the go-to option for now?

Thanks in advance

*EDIT* Just a quick clarification, not that this probably matters but I will be using RStan to do this

Martin Flores

messages.subject_clean: function libraries with the C++ preprocessor
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

For anyone who wants to use this include stuff with cmdstan more systematic: Just add into make/local two lines like

%.stan : %.tstan
        $(CC) -x c++ -E $< -o $@

Note, that the space before "$(CC)" must be a tab! Then you can write in the future instead of .stan files .tstan files. When you build the model executables as usual, the above make rule will turn the .tstan in a .stan file file the pre-processor being run over it. You may want to toss in some more options to your preprocessor to point the program to a location where you stored you to-be-included stan snippets, haven't figure that out.

If you want to continue use # as comment character, then you would have to add in another sed command above.

I find it really useful, but this is not a "Stan-standard".

Cheers,
Sebastian

messages.subject: speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.subject_clean: speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

in the stan language reference a zero inflation model is described as follows:

for (n in 1:N) {
  if (y[n] == 0)
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_log(1,theta),
                                                     bernoulli_log(0,theta)
                                                     + poisson_log(y[n],lambda)));
  else
    increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0,theta)
                                 + poisson_log(y[n],lambda));
}

I was thinking of improving the speed of the model by
- splitting the array y in two parts,
  one where y = 0 and the other where y != 0
- putting the results of
  log_sum_exp(bernoulli_log(1,theta),
                      bernoulli_log(0,theta)
                      + poisson_log(y[n],lambda))
  and
  bernoulli_log(0,theta) + poisson_log(y[n],lambda)
  into two vectors log_prob_y and log_prob_y0
- and finally pass the vectors log_prob_y
  and log_prob_y0 to increment_log_prob

The underlying idea is to vectorize as much as possible.
For example when calculating log_prob_y and log_prob_y0,
I would "vectorize" for bernoulli_log and poisson_log or
neg_binomial_2_lo_log. The only place where one would
still have to loop is for log_sum_exp.

I am unsure if such a modification would would improve
the speed noticeable, because if I understand it correctly
calculating the gradients is the most time consuming operation,
and I do not understand if the changes I suggested have any
influence on the calculation of gradients.

Thanks in advance!
Guido

PS: In my particular case the data set is moderately large
(N = 50 000 rows and 20 predictors) and I am using the
negative binomial model.
An improvement in speed of 10% would already be useful for me!

Check out chapter 13 in the 2.9.0 manual on sparse and
ragged data structures (I don't know the chapter number in
earlier version).  The key idea is to treat it like
a database rather than a matrix with missing values or
a ragged array.  Let us know if you still have questions
after reading through that.

I don't have a reference offhand, but there have been
examples posted of how to most efficiently code Kronecker
products in Stan now.

The problem with defining them directly is that you really
want to use a C++ expression template on the back end and
Eigen, our template library, doesn't support them.  I believe
one idea is to code up the compound Kronecker product and
downstream operation, which is most efficient, but can be
combinatorially prohibitive if there are lots of places
Kronecker might be used.

- Bob

messages.subject: Inconsistent timing for HMC runs
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistent timing for HMC runs
messages.body_plain:
I noticed when using Stan to run HMC that there was a lot of variation in the sampling time of my models. I ran a quick test of this, taking the 8-schools model and running it across a int_time of 1 to 20 and a 20 different seeds. As it turns out, the timings for the warmup period are very consistent and scale with int_time as expected. However, the sampling time was indeed very variable. Further, I ran NUTS with the same seeds and took the mean of the n_leapfrog__ for the warmup and sampling periods and that doesn't match the same pattern as HMC. Below is some quick simulation code.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-bkHu-0CCvWM/Vnsab8mOLaI/AAAAAAAAAAM/R5Y94hXbdtI/s1600/stan_speed_tests.png>

>From what I understand of these algorithms, particularly HMC, the core computational costs are the leapfrog algorithm, and even if the algorithm rejected every proposal it should take the same time as one that accepted every proposal.

This raises several questions:
Why would the sampling period for HMC be variable when the warmup was not (both were the same number of iterations)?
Shouldn't HMC be very consistent and scale directly with int_time?
Shouldn't the NUTS algorithm take the same time as HMC given the same number of total leapfrog steps?
Shouldn't the timing be independent of the tuning parameters, given total leapfrog steps?
Am I missing something obvious here?
System Info:
R version 3.2.2 (2015-08-14)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
Running under: Windows 8 x64 (build 9200)
Rstan=2.8.2
Rtools gcc= 4.6.3

Here's code to reproduce this test, using the 8schools.stan model.
## Speed tests for Stan algorithms. HMC should scale linearly with int_time
## and NUTS should be similar for average n_leapfrog__ for the warmup and
## sampling period.
seeds <- 1:20
int_time <- seq(1,20, by=2)
Nsim <- 5000
schools_dat <- list(J=8, y=c(28,8,-3,7,-1,1,18,12), sigma=c(15,10,16,11,9,11,10,18))
fit <- stan(file='schools/schools.stan', data=schools_dat, iter=10,
                chains=1, seed=seed, algorithm='HMC', control=list(int_time=1))
speed.hmc <-
  ldply(seeds, function(seed){
          fit.hmc <- ldply(int_time, function(L){
                    fit <- stan(fit=fit, data=schools_dat, iter=Nsim,
                                chains=1, seed=seed, algorithm='HMC', control=list(int_time=L))
                    data.frame(L=L, seed=seed, rstan::get_elapsed_time(fit))
                    })})
speed.nuts <-
  ldply(seeds, function(seed){
          fit <- stan(fit=fit, data=schools_dat, iter=Nsim,
                      chains=1, seed=seed, algorithm='NUTS')
          temp <- data.frame(get_sampler_params(fit))
          data.frame(warmup.nleap=mean(temp[(1:Nsim/2), 'n_leapfrog__']),
                          sample.nleap=mean(temp[-(1:Nsim/2),'n_leapfrog__']),
                          get_elapsed_time(fit), seed=seed)})
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(warmup~L, data=speed.hmc, ylab="Time", xlab="Steps", main='Warmup',
     ylim=c(0, max(speed.hmc$sample)))
points(warmup~warmup.nleap, data=speed.nuts, col='red', pch=2)
plot(sample~L, data=speed.hmc, ylab="Time", xlab="Steps", main='Sample',
     ylim=c(0, max(speed.hmc$sample)))
points(sample~sample.nleap, data=speed.nuts, col='red', pch=2)
legend('topleft', legend=c("HMC", "NUTS"), col=c('black', 'red'), pch=c(1,2))

messages.subject: Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
messages.subject_clean: Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Apologies in advance for a somewhat imprecise and arm-waving question, but I wanted to throw this out there and see if anyone else is noticing something similar. I've been working on a couple of fairly involved projects in Stan and making great progress, thanks in large part to this wonderful community of Stan developers and fellow users. I had been running RStan 2.8.0 on R version 3.2.2 until yesterday, when I upgraded to RStan 2.8.2 (I missed 2.8.1) and R version 3.2.3. Since upgrading, I am getting much slower runtimes -- around 3x-4x longer than previously. I've reproduced this on two different Windows 7 machines, and no other changes were made to either system.

I realize the simultaneous R and RStan upgrades make this a badly designed "experiment", but here's what I've tried, in various combinations: (1) restarting my R session, (2) rebooting Windows, (3) removing and reinstalling RStan (always from CRAN via install.packages() and following the steps on the RStan Getting Started guide, including setting optimization level -O3), and (4) uninstalling and reinstalling Rtools (version 3.3.0.1959), always making sure to allow the installer to edit the PATH variable. None of this has made a difference to the ultra-slow performance. I have not yet tried reverting to R 3.2.2 and/or RStan 2.8.0, in part because I'm hoping this issue can be resolved and in part because I have the impression that reverting to old versions of RStan is not super straightforward. I'm willing to try either of these options if that's what it takes to diagnose the problem, though. I'm also happy to provide any R session info or other details that may help track this down.

Like I said, mainly I just wanted to see if anyone else was experiencing this, and if anyone has any suggestions.

Many thanks,
EB

Thanks Dr. Carpenter. I glossed over that section my first time through the documentation because I saw a similar example where the person used a ragged array type coding, but after reading through more carefully I can see why treating it like a database makes more sense.

Martin Flores

On Wednesday, December 23, 2015 at 12:59:45 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Check out chapter 13 in the 2.9.0 manual on sparse and
> ragged data structures (I don't know the chapter number in
> earlier version).  The key idea is to treat it like
> a database rather than a matrix with missing values or
> a ragged array.  Let us know if you still have questions
> after reading through that.
>
> I don't have a reference offhand, but there have been
> examples posted of how to most efficiently code Kronecker
> products in Stan now.
>
> The problem with defining them directly is that you really
> want to use a C++ expression template on the back end and
> Eigen, our template library, doesn't support them.  I believe
> one idea is to code up the compound Kronecker product and
> downstream operation, which is most efficient, but can be
> combinatorially prohibitive if there are lots of places
> Kronecker might be used.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Dec 23, 2015, at 2:20 AM, mjfl...@g.ucla.edu wrote:
> >
> > Hey everyone,
> > I'm pretty new to Stan, and I've been going through the documentation to figure out how to code up a longitudinal factor analysis where the number of time points differs from individual to individual, and the points are unequally spaced. Suppose for example we have two people, the first of whom has two observations, and the second of whom has three. Also suppose that we have 5 outcomes and two factors for each observation. There are two issues I'm not entirely sure how to deal with. Letting i index people, j index time points, k index the outcomes, and p index the factors, (my outcomes are a mix of binaries and counts, so I have to define a custom probability function)
> >
> > The first is that I'm not sure what is the most reasonable way to declare the outcomes y_ijk and factors f_ijp. I was thinking about defining a single array/vector for all the outcomes using code from the documentation
> >
> > data {
> > int<lower=0> N; // # people
> > int s[J]; // number of records per person
> > int<lower=0> K; // # of outcomes
> > int<lower=0> P; // # of factors
> > vector[N*sum(s)] y; // observations (i don't think this syntax is correct, but hopefully it's clear what I'm trying to accomplish with this)
> >
> > where y would just be a column vector that looks like
> >
> > y_111
> > y_112
> > .
> > .
> > .
> > y_234
> > y_235
> >
> > and then just segment it twice, once to take out all the observations for person 1, and then another time to get the observations for person 1 at time j
> >
> > model{
> >   int pos.person;
> >   int pos.time;
> >   pos.person <- 1;
> >   for(i in 1:N){
> >     pos.time <- 1;
> >     for(j in 1:s[i]){
> >       ysub <- segment(segment(y,pos.person,s[i]*K),pos.time,pos.time+K-1) // Vector containing the jth measurement for person i
> >       increment_log_prob(X) // X is going to be a custom probability function for the entries of ysub
> >       pos.time <- pos.time + K
> >     }
> >     pos.person <- pos.person + s[i]*K
> >   }
> > }
> >
> > I don't think the syntax is completely correct, but the basic idea is just taking all of the outcomes for all of the individuals at all of the time points, stacking them, and then just defining the density on subsets of that vector as per page 145 of the documentation.
> >
> > I know that if my data were really this simple that I could just define vectors y_11 up to y_23, but my actual data has upwards of 10,000 records and 100 outcomes which is why I'm trying to find another way to do this. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Inconsistent timing for HMC runs
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Inconsistent timing for HMC runs
messages.body_plain:
Firstly, when including figures please make sure that they are large enough to at least
read the axis labels easily enough.

Secondly, let me be a bit pedantic regarding names.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)
is a very generic way of generating high-performance Markov chains.  NUTS is one
_implementation_ of HMC.  As is _static HMC_, which uses a constant integration
time and takes the final point as a proposal.  In your comparisons you are comparing
static HMC with NUTS.

Thirdly, integration time is not equal to the number of leapfrog steps.  Rather integration
time is the product of the integrator step size and total number of leapfrog steps, so
n_leapfrog = int_time / epsilon.  Also, the mean n_leapfrog in NUTS isn’t particularly
helpful due to the typical skewness of the distribution.

Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters
being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
leads to varying performance.

Long story short, to do a proper comparison you’ll want to turn adaptation off to ensure
the same tuning parameters and make sure to compare the number of leapfrog steps
and not the integration time.

> Why would the sampling period for HMC be variable when the warmup was not (both were the same number of iterations)?

Because of adaptation in warmup.  See the manual for a discussion of our windowed
adaptation procedure.  In particular, with iter=10 you have only 5 warmup iterations
which will update the mass matrix only once, after the fifth iteration.  If you use a
much more reasonable warmup then you’ll start to see variation in warmup timings,
too.

> Shouldn't HMC be very consistent and scale directly with int_time?

Practical implementations of HMC use numerical integrators, which imply that the
algorithms should scales with the number of leapfrog steps, not integration time
directly.

> Shouldn't the NUTS algorithm take the same time as HMC given the same number of total leapfrog steps?

Transition by transition, yes, if you ignore algorithmic overhead.  But that doesn’t
mean that they will when you average over chains set to different tunings.

> Shouldn't the timing be independent of the tuning parameters, given total leapfrog steps?

If you could set the total leapfrog steps then yes.  But you can’t do that in any of
our samplers right now.

I'm not sure what "essentially noiseless".  Either y = a + b, or it equals a + b + noise.

If it's the latter, then you want to fit what noise is there in the data.

The problem is that if just a and b are scalars, then your model isn't
identified.  See the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual for
just this example.

And you can't fit a prior based on one obseration.  Are a and b
supposed to be vectors?

Maybe I should use the modeling approach you suggest and place a strong prior on sigma that keeps it very close to zero?  It seems that any non-zero-ness of sigma, however, would hurt my estimates of the parameters of the distributions from which a and b come.

The big problem is that if a and b really are scalars, then every
value has to be the same.

> The immediate problem is that you’re trying to assign a scalar (a + b)

the shower and how long the shower lasts.

Can you assume exactly one shower/day?
