messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael, thanks for this information.

I'm interested in these details b/c in my field there are other software packages that use HMC/NUTS and I want to do some comparisons with Stan. I read the NUTS paper carefully and coded it and static HMC from scratch. For some reason I assumed that int_time in Stan must be the number of steps and not integration time, so that clarifies many things.  I'll respond inline below and hope you have time to answer some more of my questions.

On Thursday, December 24, 2015 at 10:25:31 AM UTC-8, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Firstly, when including figures please make sure that they are large enough to at least
> read the axis labels easily enough.
>

I was just using the defaults for the web interface and figured a thumbnail would be fine since you could click on it and get the full version. I'll attach it full size next time.

> Secondly, let me be a bit pedantic regarding names.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)
> is a very generic way of generating high-performance Markov chains.  NUTS is one
> _implementation_ of HMC.  As is _static HMC_, which uses a constant integration
> time and takes the final point as a proposal.  In your comparisons you are comparing
> static HMC with NUTS.
>

Fair enough, but suspect most users won't make that distinction b/c that's how you specify them in Stan.

> Thirdly, integration time is not equal to the number of leapfrog steps.  Rather integration
> time is the product of the integrator step size and total number of leapfrog steps, so
> n_leapfrog = int_time / epsilon.  Also, the mean n_leapfrog in NUTS isn’t particularly
> helpful due to the typical skewness of the distribution.
>

It seems most other software programs with HMC (e.g., ADMB), as well as the papers describing it, you specify step size and number of steps. I think it might be worth explaining this in the adaptation section of the manual. The term int_time isn't used at all there, not really described in the help files in Rstan. I thought using mean n_leapfrog for NUTS would be reasonable b/c it is the total steps divided by the number of iterations. I reran with the n_leapfrog calculated as above and plotted that instead of int_time and it totally makes sense now (attached here).

> Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters
> being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
> differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
> adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
> leads to varying performance.
>

Neal (2011) describes two ways of using the mass matrix:  a Chloesky decomposition of parameter space or using it in the kinetic energy function. The first seems to be more population. Does Stan use the mass matrix to do a Cholesky decomposition? Is that why there are such computational differences depending on tuning parameters? Are the differences only in unit vs. diagonal vs. dense matrices, or can there also be differences between different dense matrices (e.g. taking advantage of sparseness)?

> Long story short, to do a proper comparison you’ll want to turn adaptation off to ensure
> the same tuning parameters and make sure to compare the number of leapfrog steps
> and not the integration time.
> > Why would the sampling period for HMC be variable when the warmup was not (both were the same number of iterations)?
> Because of adaptation in warmup.  See the manual for a discussion of our windowed
> adaptation procedure.  In particular, with iter=10 you have only 5 warmup iterations
> which will update the mass matrix only once, after the fifth iteration.  If you use a
> much more reasonable warmup then you’ll start to see variation in warmup timings,
> too.

I only used iter=10 to build the model once and then used 2500 warmup and 2500 sampling iterations for the actual analyses. If the variance in computational time is due to the adaptive mass matrix, then the last period of the warmup should be similar to the sampling period. I'll check that.

> > Shouldn't HMC be very consistent and scale directly with int_time?
> Practical implementations of HMC use numerical integrators, which imply that the
> algorithms should scales with the number of leapfrog steps, not integration time
> directly.
> > Shouldn't the NUTS algorithm take the same time as HMC given the same number of total leapfrog steps?
> Transition by transition, yes, if you ignore algorithmic overhead.  But that doesn’t
> mean that they will when you average over chains set to different tunings.
> > Shouldn't the timing be independent of the tuning parameters, given total leapfrog steps?
> If you could set the total leapfrog steps then yes.  But you can’t do that in any of
> our samplers right now.

I think it would be valuable for the user to be able to specify the number of steps opposed to the integration time. For instance Langevin sampling can't be done directly in Stan (if I understand correctly). I could see that being potentially useful for some people in some models. What was the reasoning behind specifying integration time instead? Also, the calculation from n_step=int_time/stepsize isn't integer.. is this value rounded up?

I'm new to Stan but really like it so far and appreciate all the development that has gone into it. I think it may be helpful to the user base to have a more thorough explanation of the adaptation procedure that is going on internally. This will be particularly true for users who come from other software platforms or have coded it themselves on specific problems. For example I couldn't find the default behavior of argument metric, or how to pass an arbitrary mass matrix.

Is it correct that this is what happens when using static HMC: (1) User gives int_time, (2) a 'reasonable' stepsize is found and from this an approximate number of leapfrog steps (L), (3) the warmup procedure begins and stepsize is updated (and hence L) using dual averaging. (4) Continue with sampling.

 Thanks,
Cole

messages.body_plain:
> Secondly, let me be a bit pedantic regarding names.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)
> > is a very generic way of generating high-performance Markov chains.  NUTS is one
> > _implementation_ of HMC.  As is _static HMC_, which uses a constant integration
> > time and takes the final point as a proposal.  In your comparisons you are comparing
> > static HMC with NUTS.
> >
> Fair enough, but suspect most users won't make that distinction b/c that's how you specify them in Stan.

It is in CmdStan, which distinguishes between algorithm (HMC) and
engine (static or NUTS).  The conventions used in RStan (and then
PyStan) were not proposed by the entire team.  This will hopefully
be remedied in the refactor.

> It seems most other software programs with HMC (e.g., ADMB), as well as the papers describing it, you specify step size and number of steps. I think it might be worth explaining this in the adaptation section of the manual. The term int_time isn't used at all there, not really described in the help files in Rstan.

And just about every implementation of HMC outside of Stan is
just a reimplementation of code in the NUTS paper or Stan itself.
Integration time is more natural, especially when trying to optimize
the various free parameters in HMC.  Trying to optimize step size
and number of leapfrog steps introduces all kinds of problems, as
evident in many, many papers.

Again, the inconsistencies between the interfaces is a known problem
and we are working to improve that.

> > Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters
> > being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
> > differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
> > adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
> > leads to varying performance.
> >
> Neal (2011) describes two ways of using the mass matrix:  a Chloesky decomposition of parameter space or using it in the kinetic energy function. The first seems to be more population. Does Stan use the mass matrix to do a Cholesky decomposition? Is that why there are such computational differences depending on tuning parameters? Are the differences only in unit vs. diagonal vs. dense matrices, or can there also be differences between different dense matrices (e.g. taking advantage of sparseness)?

Those are two reparameterizations of the same problem, one is
really not different from the other in practice.  The computational
consequence is on how well-chosen the mass matrix is with
respect to the target distribution.

Stan estimates an optimal mass matrix (really Euclidean metric)
in windows during warmup, updating the mass matrix to the best
current estimate at the end of each window.

> I think it would be valuable for the user to be able to specify the number of steps opposed to the integration time.

No, it would not.  The optimal value of the number of leapfrog
steps depends on the step size — in other words only the
integration time and step size can be optimized independently
of each other.  People keep making this mistake in the literature
and it causes no end of confusion that we (often I) have to clean
up.

> For instance Langevin sampling can't be done directly in Stan (if I understand correctly). I could see that being potentially useful for some people in some models.

There is no reason for ever using Langevin over HMC — if there
were I can assure you that it would be in Stan.  We’re not just
implementing algorithms here, we’re also the ones actively
researching them.

> What was the reasoning behind specifying integration time instead?

See above.

> Also, the calculation from n_step=int_time/stepsize isn't integer.. is this value rounded up?

It rounds per the implementation of C++,
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/mcmc/hmc/static/base_static_hmc.hpp

>
>
> I'm new to Stan but really like it so far and appreciate all the development that has gone into it. I think it may be helpful to the user base to have a more thorough explanation of the adaptation procedure that is going on internally. This will be particularly true for users who come from other software platforms or have coded it themselves on specific problems. For example I couldn't find the default behavior of argument metric, or how to pass an arbitrary mass matrix.

See Section 57.2 of the manual.  This is all extensively documented, and any
confusion can be resolved by looking at the code directly.

> Is it correct that this is what happens when using static HMC: (1) User gives int_time, (2) a 'reasonable' stepsize is found and from this an approximate number of leapfrog steps (L), (3) the warmup procedure begins and stepsize is updated (and hence L) using dual averaging. (4) Continue with sampling.

The initial step size in (2) does not depend on the choice of integration time.
It uses the error from a single step.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for taking the time to give us such detailed comments.

Did we manage to give you enough info to answer your original
list of questions about variability of run times?

If you look at the evaluation in the original NUTS paper,
you'll see that it's given in terms of epsilon * L, which
is integration time (less rounding);  for each integration
time, an ideal step size was estimated based on rejection rate.
It took a lot of cluster computing to generate those figures.

As Michael indicated, we're working toward unifying the interfaces,
with the big change targeted for Stan 3.   That should also allow
more control over specifying mass matrices; but we think that's
only going to be useful for stopping and restarting.

We're also continuing to work on the manual --- I think we should
be able to put in much more algorithm description before referring
people to the code (though that's the best we have now and will
always be the final arbiter of what Stan actually does in practice).

Michael --- isn't Langevin just 1 step of HMC?  And if so, for a fixed
step size (discretization interval), couldn't we just fix integration time
to be one step and get Langevin?

- Bob

> which will update the mass matrix only once, after the fifth iteration.  If you use a
> much more reasonable warmup then you’ll start to see variation in warmup timings,
> too.
>

> algorithms should scales with the number of leapfrog steps, not integration time
> directly.

> mean that they will when you average over chains set to different tunings.

messages.body_plain:
> Michael --- isn't Langevin just 1 step of HMC?

Yup.  Well, the “Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Algorithm”
is if you really want to be pedantic.

> And if so, for a fixed step size (discretization interval),
> couldn't we just fix integration time to be one step and get Langevin?

If the step size is fixed then you could do int_time = epsilon.
Or, noting that the minimum number of leapfrog steps is 1,
you could also set int_time to something really small and
for any reasonable adapted step size you’d still get Langevin.

But just because you _could_ do it doesn’t mean that you should….

It took me a while to come around to this idea that Stan is trying to do best-in-class algorithms and while it might be nice to have pure MH for completeness it would mean a lot of maintenance and it's not worth it given that we have HMC.  A lot of people just aren't going to have the background to understand that, for example, slice sampling and MH don't make sense since we have HMC but ADVI and optimization have different enough properties that they're worth including.

I just looked at the Stan manual and it doesn't really address the choice of algorithms in any clear section (maybe it's in the intro in story form) so maybe right before section 1.5 which launches into talking about sampling there could be a little section about choice of algorithms.

Krzysztof

Hi Michael, I'm probably being dense here but I'm still missing the point why specifying integration time is better than L (and let me know if this is the wrong forum to discuss these matters). For a given int_time there are different combinations of eps and L that get you there, and obviously we prefer smaller L computationally. The approach used by Stan (as in Alg 5 of the NUTS paper) will end with a different L after adaptation for different starting seeds/initial conditions, and some of those L's will be larger than others. Why wouldn't it be preferable to force L to be smaller (fix it) and let eps be bigger to get the same int_time? I'm not trying to say you should adapt both L and eps, but rather fix L.

Also, could you point me toward some studies comparing efficiency of Langevin, HMC and NUTS? Outside of the NUTS paper I've only been able to find theory and derivation of the algorithms.

On Sun, Dec 27, 2015 at 4:34 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Secondly, let me be a bit pedantic regarding names.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)
> > > is a very generic way of generating high-performance Markov chains.  NUTS is one
> > > _implementation_ of HMC.  As is _static HMC_, which uses a constant integration
> > > time and takes the final point as a proposal.  In your comparisons you are comparing
> > > static HMC with NUTS.
> > >
> > Fair enough, but suspect most users won't make that distinction b/c that's how you specify them in Stan.
>
> It is in CmdStan, which distinguishes between algorithm (HMC) and
> engine (static or NUTS).  The conventions used in RStan (and then
> PyStan) were not proposed by the entire team.  This will hopefully
> be remedied in the refactor.
>
> > It seems most other software programs with HMC (e.g., ADMB), as well as the papers describing it, you specify step size and number of steps. I think it might be worth explaining this in the adaptation section of the manual. The term int_time isn't used at all there, not really described in the help files in Rstan.
>
> And just about every implementation of HMC outside of Stan is
> just a reimplementation of code in the NUTS paper or Stan itself.
> Integration time is more natural, especially when trying to optimize
> the various free parameters in HMC.  Trying to optimize step size
> and number of leapfrog steps introduces all kinds of problems, as
> evident in many, many papers.
>
> Again, the inconsistencies between the interfaces is a known problem
> and we are working to improve that.
>
> > > Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters
> > > being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
> > > differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
> > > adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
> > > leads to varying performance.
> > >
> > Neal (2011) describes two ways of using the mass matrix:  a Chloesky decomposition of parameter space or using it in the kinetic energy function. The first seems to be more population. Does Stan use the mass matrix to do a Cholesky decomposition? Is that why there are such computational differences depending on tuning parameters? Are the differences only in unit vs. diagonal vs. dense matrices, or can there also be differences between different dense matrices (e.g. taking advantage of sparseness)?
>
> Those are two reparameterizations of the same problem, one is
> really not different from the other in practice.  The computational
> consequence is on how well-chosen the mass matrix is with
> respect to the target distribution.
>
> Stan estimates an optimal mass matrix (really Euclidean metric)
> in windows during warmup, updating the mass matrix to the best
> current estimate at the end of each window.
>
> > I think it would be valuable for the user to be able to specify the number of steps opposed to the integration time.
>
> No, it would not.  The optimal value of the number of leapfrog
> steps depends on the step size — in other words only the
> integration time and step size can be optimized independently
> of each other.  People keep making this mistake in the literature
> and it causes no end of confusion that we (often I) have to clean
> up.

>
> > For instance Langevin sampling can't be done directly in Stan (if I understand correctly). I could see that being potentially useful for some people in some models.
>
> There is no reason for ever using Langevin over HMC — if there
> were I can assure you that it would be in Stan.  We’re not just
> implementing algorithms here, we’re also the ones actively
> researching them.
>
> > What was the reasoning behind specifying integration time instead?
>
> See above.
>
> > Also, the calculation from n_step=int_time/stepsize isn't integer.. is this value rounded up?
>
> It rounds per the implementation of C++,
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/mcmc/hmc/static/base_static_hmc.hpp
> >
> >

>
> See Section 57.2 of the manual.  This is all extensively documented, and any

Was that the wrong link?

That paper talks about random-walk Metropolis, which is
a terrible algorithm.  Also, I don't think their proposed variant
will work, because (a) you need to regularize for positive definiteness (e.g.,
see Michael's paper on Softabs), and (b) with varying curvature, the
Hessian changes, and it defeats detailed balance.  There's no further description

et al.'s book in section 2.3.2.

> and there's a community of scientists that are used to its way of doing things, who likely will migrate over to Stan. I think it's worthwhile for those users (me included, obviously) to be able to notice/understand the differences and improvements to ease that transition.

That'd be great from our perspective.  We can explain Stan, but
I don't know ADMB.  If you want to write a Stan tutorial for ADMB
users, we're more than happy to help out and advertise on Andrew's
blog.

Andrew's pushing us to use Laplace approximations, both for
penalized/marginal maximum likelihood and for black-box
variational inference, but there's no reason to do that (and
lots of reasons not to) in cases where MCMC will work.

Does Stan use the mass matrix to do a Cholesky decomposition? Is that why there are such computational differences depending on tuning parameters? Are the differences only in unit vs. diagonal vs. dense matrices, or can there also be differences between different dense matrices (e.g. taking advantage of sparseness)?

messages.body_plain:
Sorry, I've been away from internet access over the holiday long weekend. Thanks to all who've weighed in.

Bob: I've been running in parallel both before and after this change, and get_cppo_mode() returns "fast" for both previously saved and newly created runs.

David: I am indeed evidently missing something, but whatever it is, I'm pretty sure it's on the R/RStan/RStudio side as opposed to the OS side. As I mentioned in the OP, I got the same behavior on two different machines after doing nothing but those three updates, and the timing is consistent (albeit not identical, of course) across multiple runs with different or identical seeds, despite restarting R and Windows, etc.

Since I can't go back in time (alas), the only controlled comparison I can think of is between a previously saved stanfit object and a new model run with exactly the same model file, inits, and seed (from get_stancode(old_fit), get_inits(old_fit), and get_seeds(old_fit), respectively), and the same runtime arguments. The seeds were the same for all three chains; I'm under the impression that distinct seeds are generated internally, but correct me if I've got this wrong. The Stan and R code, data, and inits are attached. Here's the timing comparison, on a 2.9 GHz quad-core i7 with 16 GB RAM:

before updates

> cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
        warmup  sample    total
chain:1 349.483 1238.97 1588.453
chain:2 354.452 1239.17 1593.622
chain:3 349.198 1240.84 1590.038

after updates

> cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
        warmup   sample    total
chain:1 526.599 3687.639 4214.238
chain:2 521.119 3078.829 3599.948
chain:3 566.603 3683.561 4250.164

Like I said, the code is a bit involved and I don't expect anyone to read it in detail. However, I should mention that the plot has thickened: I did the same experiment with a different previously saved model, and in that case I found no consistent difference in timing! That model takes ~3 h to run, and the pre- and post-update timing was not identical, but the differences were minor and inconsistent in direction and could easily be due to differences in system activity, etc. So it seems there is some sort of model x software version interaction going on here.

To be clear, I'm not trying to lay this issue at Stan's doorstep, and I hope I haven't seemed to suggest otherwise. I have no idea what's going on, and it could certainly be some subtle interaction between R and Stan. Maybe this is beyond the purview of the stan-users group, and that's okay. As I said in the OP, I just found it hard to believe that I'm the only one who's seeing this (on two machines), and I wanted to try and compare notes with others.

Thanks,
Eric

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
messages.body_plain:
Multivariate probit is fundamental to the application in question, because you really are interested in the underlying latent variables -- or at least their joint distribution. This kind of thing shows up a lot in marketing research where you have latent variables interpreted as an individual's utility for some product or choice option, and all you can actually observe are their choices, which in this application tells you whether the latent variable was greater than a threshold, and in other applications tells you which of several latent variables has the greatest value.

Note that the problem in this instance is not that the individual MCMC iterations are slow -- it's that the chain is mixing slowly, much more slowly than I am used to seeing with Stan, and this is with only a five-dimensional multivariate normal distribution on the latent vectors.

> There’s also the option of stepping back and thinking harder about the model.  It is possible that this researcher wants a latent multivariable distribution, in which case Stan as currently configured will run slow (although longer-term I have hope for a MML or VB approach that can rapidly approximate over the latent variables).  It is also possible that the data could be modeled more directly, in which case the fit will probably be easier.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
messages.body_plain:
Multinomial probit and multivariate probit both involve computing rectangular probabilities

    Pr(a[1] <= x[1] <= b[1] and ... and a[n] <= x[n] <= b[n])

for multivariate normal distributions, and this is computationally difficult for any n beyond 2, or maybe 3. The GHK algorithm is sometimes used here, but it is a low-accuracy Monte Carlo algorithm, and when you try to use it within MCMC you generally get a smeared-out and distorted posterior. This, and the fact that the latent variables generally have a meaningful interpretation, is why augmenting with latent variables is often used in such models.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] modeling observation as a function of two random quantities
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Thanks for your continued thought on this question.

On Saturday, December 26, 2015 at 9:15:52 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The standard thing to do would be to model when he starts
> the shower and how long the shower lasts.

That could get hairy because we both arrive at work at highly erratic times -- some days I arrive early for an early meeting, other days I sleep in, other days I arrive in the afternoon, etc.  I can't say anything about the distribution of my arrival time or the distribution of his arrival time.

> Can you assume exactly one shower/day?

Maybe one shower per day, but certainly not one observation per day.  If I arrive at the locker room before this guy, I take my shower and go on with my day and don't observe anything about his shower duration.  If I arrive after his shower is done, I don't observe anything about his shower duration.  So I would say a maximum of one observation per day.  Most days no observation at all.

> Anything you know about when it is and how long it is
> a priori?

I summarize my prior information (based on knowledge of how long it takes most humans to shower) in the following way.

prior on mean shower duration is truncated normal, centered on 15, with sd = 5, left-truncation at 0 and no right-truncation.

prior on precision of shower duration is gamma(0.2, 0.1).  I would be happy with any not-too-informative prior here.  I know half-t has been recommended in some cases.

> What exactly do you observe?

Only how long I wait.

> Arrival time and if or if
> not a shower going on?

No.

> Do you have shower end time if
> you arrive during the shower?

No, but I know how long I waited.  If I make a new clock and start it when I arrive, then on that clock's time, I have the shower end time.

> Shower start and end time
> if you arrive before the shower?

No observation if I arrive before he starts the shower.

> If you always arrive during a shower and don't observe
> when showers end, you won't be able to estimate duration
> because the model won't be identifiable.

How can you tell that it's non-identifiable?  Oftentimes, when I believe a model is non-identifiable, I try to think of two parameter sets that have the same probability distribution.  But I haven't been able to think of any for this problem yet.

> Otherwise, you
> have censoring of a start or end time --- see the chapter
> on censored data in the model.
>
> - Bob
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob, a few thoughts inline below...

On Mon, Dec 28, 2015 at 12:34 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Dec 28, 2015, at 1:25 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob, yes I've got my questions answered for the most part. It's been a useful discussion in that I've learned a lot. I think it's worth noting that ADMB coupled AD and static HMC (using inverse Hessian as mass matrix) probably a decade ago
>
> I didn't see any mention of HMC in that paper.
> Was that the wrong link?
>
> That paper talks about random-walk Metropolis, which is
> a terrible algorithm.  Also, I don't think their proposed variant
> will work, because (a) you need to regularize for positive definiteness (e.g.,
> see Michael's paper on Softabs), and (b) with varying curvature, the
> Hessian changes, and it defeats detailed balance.  There's no further description
> of the algorithm or adjustments made for soundness, only a pointer to Gelman
> et al.'s book in section 2.3.2.
>

I was a bit too brief. ADMB was essentially written by a single person and then was recently bought and turned open source. It was/is designed for maximum likelihood estimation with MCMC capabilities tacked on (since why not?). It's amazingly robust and fast at optimization. If the Hessian at the mode is positive definite it will use the inverse for the RWM multivariate normal, or the mass matrix for the static HMC. To be clear it uses a fixed mass matrix avoiding issues above. It does indeed have static HMC it's just poorly documented, but you can see the details in the code here <http://admb-project.org/documentation/api/hybmcmc_8cpp_source.html>. I became interested in HMC because RWM was so slow for our big, tough models. Part of my dissertation research (hopefully) is to bring these new methods to our field.

> > and there's a community of scientists that are used to its way of doing things, who likely will migrate over to Stan. I think it's worthwhile for those users (me included, obviously) to be able to notice/understand the differences and improvements to ease that transition.
>
> That'd be great from our perspective.  We can explain Stan, but
> I don't know ADMB.  If you want to write a Stan tutorial for ADMB
> users, we're more than happy to help out and advertise on Andrew's
> blog.

Yes I could do that, should I fork stan-dev and then do a pull request? ADMB and Stan are actually very similar so a few examples of ADMB models in Stan would go a long way. As part of my research I'll be coding lots of models in both so it would be easy to throw together a quick guide with examples.

>
> Andrew's pushing us to use Laplace approximations, both for
> penalized/marginal maximum likelihood and for black-box
> variational inference, but there's no reason to do that (and
> lots of reasons not to) in cases where MCMC will work.
>

There's also TMB <http://arxiv.org/abs/1509.00660> which is similar to ADMB but has Laplace approximations built in. I'm also trying to recreate basic HMC algorithms for it too.

-Cole

> - Bob
>
>
> >
> > I look forward to Stan 3 to see the changes. In the meantime I've got my original questions answered.
> >
> > Thanks
> > Cole
> >
> > On Sun, Dec 27, 2015 at 7:24 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > Thanks for taking the time to give us such detailed comments.
> >
> > Did we manage to give you enough info to answer your original
> > list of questions about variability of run times?
> >
> > If you look at the evaluation in the original NUTS paper,
> > you'll see that it's given in terms of epsilon * L, which
> > is integration time (less rounding);  for each integration
> > time, an ideal step size was estimated based on rejection rate.
> > It took a lot of cluster computing to generate those figures.
> >
> > As Michael indicated, we're working toward unifying the interfaces,
> > with the big change targeted for Stan 3.   That should also allow
> > more control over specifying mass matrices; but we think that's
> > only going to be useful for stopping and restarting.
> >
> > We're also continuing to work on the manual --- I think we should
> > be able to put in much more algorithm description before referring
> > people to the code (though that's the best we have now and will
> > always be the final arbiter of what Stan actually does in practice).
> >
> > Michael --- isn't Langevin just 1 step of HMC?  And if so, for a fixed
> > step size (discretization interval), couldn't we just fix integration time
> > to be one step and get Langevin?
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Dec 27, 2015, at 6:41 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Michael, thanks for this information.
> > >
> > > I'm interested in these details b/c in my field there are other software packages that use HMC/NUTS and I want to do some comparisons with Stan. I read the NUTS paper carefully and coded it and static HMC from scratch. For some reason I assumed that int_time in Stan must be the number of steps and not integration time, so that clarifies many things.  I'll respond inline below and hope you have time to answer some more of my questions.
> > >
> > > On Thursday, December 24, 2015 at 10:25:31 AM UTC-8, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > Firstly, when including figures please make sure that they are large enough to at least
> > > read the axis labels easily enough.
> > >
> > > I was just using the defaults for the web interface and figured a thumbnail would be fine since you could click on it and get the full version. I'll attach it full size next time.
> > >
> > > Secondly, let me be a bit pedantic regarding names.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)
> > > is a very generic way of generating high-performance Markov chains.  NUTS is one
> > > _implementation_ of HMC.  As is _static HMC_, which uses a constant integration
> > > time and takes the final point as a proposal.  In your comparisons you are comparing
> > > static HMC with NUTS.
> > >
> > > Fair enough, but suspect most users won't make that distinction b/c that's how you specify them in Stan.
> > >
> > > Thirdly, integration time is not equal to the number of leapfrog steps.  Rather integration
> > > time is the product of the integrator step size and total number of leapfrog steps, so
> > > n_leapfrog = int_time / epsilon.  Also, the mean n_leapfrog in NUTS isn’t particularly
> > > helpful due to the typical skewness of the distribution.
> > >
> > > It seems most other software programs with HMC (e.g., ADMB), as well as the papers describing it, you specify step size and number of steps. I think it might be worth explaining this in the adaptation section of the manual. The term int_time isn't used at all there, not really described in the help files in Rstan. I thought using mean n_leapfrog for NUTS would be reasonable b/c it is the total steps divided by the number of iterations. I reran with the n_leapfrog calculated as above and plotted that instead of int_time and it totally makes sense now (attached here).
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters
> > > being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
> > > differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
> > > adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
> > > leads to varying performance.
> > >
> > > Neal (2011) describes two ways of using the mass matrix:  a Chloesky decomposition of parameter space or using it in the kinetic energy function. The first seems to be more population. Does Stan use the mass matrix to do a Cholesky decomposition? Is that why there are such computational differences depending on tuning parameters? Are the differences only in unit vs. diagonal vs. dense matrices, or can there also be differences between different dense matrices (e.g. taking advantage of sparseness)?
> > >
> > > Long story short, to do a proper comparison you’ll want to turn adaptation off to ensure
> > > the same tuning parameters and make sure to compare the number of leapfrog steps
> > > and not the integration time.
> > >>      • Why would the sampling period for HMC be variable when the warmup was not (both were the same number of iterations)?
> > > Because of adaptation in warmup.  See the manual for a discussion of our windowed
> > > adaptation procedure.  In particular, with iter=10 you have only 5 warmup iterations
> > > which will update the mass matrix only once, after the fifth iteration.  If you use a
> > > much more reasonable warmup then you’ll start to see variation in warmup timings,
> > > too.
> > >
> > > I only used iter=10 to build the model once and then used 2500 warmup and 2500 sampling iterations for the actual analyses. If the variance in computational time is due to the adaptive mass matrix, then the last period of the warmup should be similar to the sampling period. I'll check that.
> > >>      • Shouldn't HMC be very consistent and scale directly with int_time?
> > > Practical implementations of HMC use numerical integrators, which imply that the
> > > algorithms should scales with the number of leapfrog steps, not integration time
> > > directly.
> > >>      • Shouldn't the NUTS algorithm take the same time as HMC given the same number of total leapfrog steps?
> > > Transition by transition, yes, if you ignore algorithmic overhead.  But that doesn’t
> > > mean that they will when you average over chains set to different tunings.
> > >>      • Shouldn't the timing be independent of the tuning parameters, given total leapfrog steps?
> > > If you could set the total leapfrog steps then yes.  But you can’t do that in any of
> > > our samplers right now.
> > >
> > > I think it would be valuable for the user to be able to specify the number of steps opposed to the integration time. For instance Langevin sampling can't be done directly in Stan (if I understand correctly). I could see that being potentially useful for some people in some models. What was the reasoning behind specifying integration time instead? Also, the calculation from n_step=int_time/stepsize isn't integer.. is this value rounded up?
> > >
> > >
> > > I'm new to Stan but really like it so far and appreciate all the development that has gone into it. I think it may be helpful to the user base to have a more thorough explanation of the adaptation procedure that is going on internally. This will be particularly true for users who come from other software platforms or have coded it themselves on specific problems. For example I couldn't find the default behavior of argument metric, or how to pass an arbitrary mass matrix.
> > >
> > > Is it correct that this is what happens when using static HMC: (1) User gives int_time, (2) a 'reasonable' stepsize is found and from this an approximate number of leapfrog steps (L), (3) the warmup procedure begins and stepsize is updated (and hence L) using dual averaging. (4) Continue with sampling.
> > >
> > >  Thanks,
> > > Cole

messages.body_plain:
I'd start by giving you both start times and
durations and using your observations as censored.
Normal would be easy to start, but you could go to
some kind of non-parametric model like a GP in the end.

All times are wall clock times.

If you arrive while he's showering, you don't know
when the shower starts, but you know when it ends.

If he arrives while you're showering, same information,
but reversed.

If you shower without seeing him, you only know his
shower started and ended before you got there or started
and ended after you get there.

Then just set up the model.

- Bob

> On Dec 29, 2015, at 12:04 AM, Robert Corty <rco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob,
>
> Thanks for your continued thought on this question.
>
>
> On Saturday, December 26, 2015 at 9:15:52 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The standard thing to do would be to model when he starts
> the shower and how long the shower lasts.
>
> That could get hairy because we both arrive at work at highly erratic times -- some days I arrive early for an early meeting, other days I sleep in, other days I arrive in the afternoon, etc.  I can't say anything about the distribution of my arrival time or the distribution of his arrival time.
>
> Can you assume exactly one shower/day?
>
> Maybe one shower per day, but certainly not one observation per day.  If I arrive at the locker room before this guy, I take my shower and go on with my day and don't observe anything about his shower duration.  If I arrive after his shower is done, I don't observe anything about his shower duration.  So I would say a maximum of one observation per day.  Most days no observation at all.
>
> Anything you know about when it is and how long it is
> a priori?
>
> I summarize my prior information (based on knowledge of how long it takes most humans to shower) in the following way.
>
> prior on mean shower duration is truncated normal, centered on 15, with sd = 5, left-truncation at 0 and no right-truncation.
>
> prior on precision of shower duration is gamma(0.2, 0.1).  I would be happy with any not-too-informative prior here.  I know half-t has been recommended in some cases.
>
>
> What exactly do you observe?
>
> Only how long I wait.
>
> Arrival time and if or if
> not a shower going on?
>
> No.
>
> Do you have shower end time if
> you arrive during the shower?
>
> No, but I know how long I waited.  If I make a new clock and start it when I arrive, then on that clock's time, I have the shower end time.
>
> Shower start and end time
> if you arrive before the shower?
>
> No observation if I arrive before he starts the shower.
>
> If you always arrive during a shower and don't observe
> when showers end, you won't be able to estimate duration
> because the model won't be identifiable.
>
> How can you tell that it's non-identifiable?  Oftentimes, when I believe a model is non-identifiable, I try to think of two parameter sets that have the same probability distribution.  But I haven't been able to think of any for this problem yet.
>
> Otherwise, you
> have censoring of a start or end time --- see the chapter
> on censored data in the model.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Dec 26, 2015, at 6:49 PM, Robert Corty <rco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Bob,
> >
> > Thanks for your help.
> >
> > On Saturday, December 26, 2015 at 1:57:36 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > > On Dec 26, 2015, at 10:50 AM, Robert Corty <rco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > Michael,
> > >
> > > Thanks for your response.  It seems that in my attempt to make a toy example of my problem, I introduced a load of simple errors that obscured the problem.
> >
> > Specifically, you can't assign a real value to a vector.
> >
> > Got it.  I believe this error is corrected in the code I included in my most recent post.
> >
> >
> > >  I can deal with all those errors, and I've included below my draft of the model I really want to build, along with an R program to simulate data for it, which I think is clean from those types of errors.
> > >
> > > The key piece of the discussion is your recommendation to add this line to the model block:
> > >
> > > w ~ normal(a + b, sigma);
> > >
> > > But I think that conveys a pretty different idea than what I'm going for.  I don't believe that my observation is the sum of a, b, and noise.  I actually believe that my observation is an essentially noiseless function of a and b.
> >
> > I'm not sure what "essentially noiseless".  Either y = a + b, or it equals a + b + noise.
> >
> > When I wrote "essentially noiseless", I meant "noiseless".  Deterministic.

messages.body_plain:
I had a similar setup as Eric so I ran the model before, and then upgraded RStudio, R and rstan to match this scenario. I was not able to recreate the differences in timings as posted.

On Monday, December 28, 2015 at 12:36:16 PM UTC-8, Eric Buhle wrote:
> Sorry, I've been away from internet access over the holiday long weekend. Thanks to all who've weighed in.
>
> Bob: I've been running in parallel both before and after this change, and get_cppo_mode() returns "fast" for both previously saved and newly created runs.
>
> David: I am indeed evidently missing something, but whatever it is, I'm pretty sure it's on the R/RStan/RStudio side as opposed to the OS side. As I mentioned in the OP, I got the same behavior on two different machines after doing nothing but those three updates, and the timing is consistent (albeit not identical, of course) across multiple runs with different or identical seeds, despite restarting R and Windows, etc.
>
> Since I can't go back in time (alas), the only controlled comparison I can think of is between a previously saved stanfit object and a new model run with exactly the same model file, inits, and seed (from get_stancode(old_fit), get_inits(old_fit), and get_seeds(old_fit), respectively), and the same runtime arguments. The seeds were the same for all three chains; I'm under the impression that distinct seeds are generated internally, but correct me if I've got this wrong. The Stan and R code, data, and inits are attached. Here's the timing comparison, on a 2.9 GHz quad-core i7 with 16 GB RAM:
>
> before updates
>
> > cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
>         warmup  sample    total
> chain:1 349.483 1238.97 1588.453
> chain:2 354.452 1239.17 1593.622
> chain:3 349.198 1240.84 1590.038
>
> after updates
>
> > cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
>         warmup   sample    total
> chain:1 526.599 3687.639 4214.238
> chain:2 521.119 3078.829 3599.948
> chain:3 566.603 3683.561 4250.164
>
> Like I said, the code is a bit involved and I don't expect anyone to read it in detail. However, I should mention that the plot has thickened: I did the same experiment with a different previously saved model, and in that case I found no consistent difference in timing! That model takes ~3 h to run, and the pre- and post-update timing was not identical, but the differences were minor and inconsistent in direction and could easily be due to differences in system activity, etc. So it seems there is some sort of model x software version interaction going on here.
>
> To be clear, I'm not trying to lay this issue at Stan's doorstep, and I hope I haven't seemed to suggest otherwise. I have no idea what's going on, and it could certainly be some subtle interaction between R and Stan. Maybe this is beyond the purview of the stan-users group, and that's okay. As I said in the OP, I just found it hard to believe that I'm the only one who's seeing this (on two machines), and I wanted to try and compare notes with others.
>
> Thanks,
> Eric
>

Andrew: Yes, I would assume so. Caveat the following with the fact I'm a student just learning all this myself... What makes ADMB so powerful is AD, a template language, and compiled C++ -- all of which Stan also has. ADMB has some additional nice features since it was designed for optimization. I could see the fishery and ecology communities moving to Stan over time but there's a ton of legacy ADMB code so that might be a slow transition. For instance, many fishery stock assessments done by the government are using a 20,000 line ADMB model (stock synthesis; Methot and Wetzel, 2011) which realistically no one is going to reproduce in Stan anytime soon.

Our field has relied on ADMB since the 1990s because it was the best (only?)  option for robust non-linear optimization at the time, so it is really exciting to see the development of Stan and what it has to offer moving forward.

> On Dec 31, 2015, at 2:40 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Stan should be just as fast for these optimization problems, no?
> A

I don't see why not.  I'm assuming our autodiff and density
library is faster and more expressive, too, but we weren't able
to get ADMB's autodiff working to test it.

>> On Dec 29, 2015, at 12:44 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
>>
>>
>> I was a bit too brief. ADMB was essentially written by a single person and then was recently bought and turned open source. It was/is designed for maximum likelihood estimation with MCMC capabilities tacked on (since why not?).

The reason not to implement Metropolis for users is that
you don't want to give them something that's going to return
the wrong answer.

This is why we're so worried about variational inference at the
moment and why it has a big "EXPERIMENTAL" tag on it.  Even in
cases where it returns an answer, we don't undrestand the properties
of the answer (either the point estimate of the approximating density
or its variance).

There are models for which Metropolis will seem to mix OK,
non-robust autocorrelation estimators like the one in Coda
(a popular R package) will be used to assess effective sample
size and miss long-term corelations, and the user will be led
to believe they've converged and can estimate posterior
expectations when in fact their results will be wrong.

>> It's amazingly robust and fast at optimization.

Optimization's relatively well understood.  At least for
convex problems.

>> If the Hessian at the mode is positive definite it will use the inverse for the RWM multivariate normal, or the mass matrix for the static HMC.

Is there a description of the algorithm somewhere?

The problem you run into with that approach is that the
mode often doesn't exist, or is not in the typical set, or the
posterior has varying curvature so that a static estimate
won't work well.  We've found a diagonal variance to be more
robust and we have to compensate by taking small step sizes so
that an iterated first-order gradient can deal with the curvature.
But that introduces problems like stiff ODE solvers.

- Bob

in C++ anyway, and we know how to test that.

> Our field has relied on ADMB since the 1990s because it was the best (only?)  option for robust non-linear optimization at the time, so it is really exciting to see the development of Stan and what it has to offer moving forward.

It's the combination of autodiff (or symbolic) gradients and
a simple language that's the key.  I also don't know of anything
other than ADMB that did that.  There were plenty of C++ and
autodiff packages, but nothing as far as I know putting them
together.  Having a big community of users, like the fisheries and
wildlife people for ADMB is also a huge benefit for everybody.

- Bob

I'm using stan-mode with emacs to edit stan source files, and I'm running into a major annoyance with indentation. When calling a user-defined function with a long function name and several arguments, I want to write

because I cannot fit the entire call on one line, but stan-mode keeps changing the indentation to

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Dec 31, 2015 at 9:23 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Dec 31, 2015, at 2:40 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Stan should be just as fast for these optimization problems, no?
> > A
>
> I don't see why not.  I'm assuming our autodiff and density
> library is faster and more expressive, too, but we weren't able
> to get ADMB's autodiff working to test it.
>
> >> On Dec 29, 2015, at 12:44 PM, Cole Monnahan <mon...@uw.edu> wrote:
> >>
> >>
> >> I was a bit too brief. ADMB was essentially written by a single person and then was recently bought and turned open source. It was/is designed for maximum likelihood estimation with MCMC capabilities tacked on (since why not?).
>
> The reason not to implement Metropolis for users is that
> you don't want to give them something that's going to return
> the wrong answer.
>
> This is why we're so worried about variational inference at the
> moment and why it has a big "EXPERIMENTAL" tag on it.  Even in
> cases where it returns an answer, we don't undrestand the properties
> of the answer (either the point estimate of the approximating density
> or its variance).
>
> There are models for which Metropolis will seem to mix OK,
> non-robust autocorrelation estimators like the one in Coda
> (a popular R package) will be used to assess effective sample
> size and miss long-term corelations, and the user will be led
> to believe they've converged and can estimate posterior
> expectations when in fact their results will be wrong.
>
> >> It's amazingly robust and fast at optimization.
>
> Optimization's relatively well understood.  At least for
> convex problems.
>
> >> If the Hessian at the mode is positive definite it will use the inverse for the RWM multivariate normal, or the mass matrix for the static HMC.
>
> Is there a description of the algorithm somewhere?

Unfortunately not really. There's a brief description in chapter 2 in the manual: http://ftp.admb-project.org/admb-11.4/manuals/admb-11.4.1.pdf but honestly the author is the only person who really understands it. I've looked at the source code enough to get the gist but there are some pieces in there that I don't understand. I can tell you there's no adaptation of HMC and for RWM there's only a global scalar for the covariance matrix that tunes the acceptance rate.

>
> The problem you run into with that approach is that the
> mode often doesn't exist, or is not in the typical set, or the
> posterior has varying curvature so that a static estimate
> won't work well.  We've found a diagonal variance to be more
> robust and we have to compensate by taking small step sizes so
> that an iterated first-order gradient can deal with the curvature.
> But that introduces problems like stiff ODE solvers.

Indeed we are familiar with these issues (which obviously affects MLE estimates as well). In these cases we simply can't do MCMC and have to change the model or abandon it. The user can specify an arbitrary covariance matrix so they can try that, but that's rare to do. We take what we can get with ADMB. This is why we're so excited by Stan.

>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: Column names for draws across estimation techniques in Rstan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

At the moment I'm estimating some models across several datasets. Depending on the size of the data, I'm using `sampling()`, `vb()` or `optimizing()`. Using them would be even easier if the outputs (parameter/generated quantities draws) were as similar as possible in terms of the column names. For instance, `optimizing()` preserves the square brackets in column names while `vb()` replaces square brackets with full stops. At the moment I'm parsing column names to re-create matrices/arrays from the draws for further simulation on new data, so it's important to me that naming is consistent.

This would seem to be a pretty small job and I'd be happy to make the changes myself and submit a pull request if someone could point me in the right direction (or give a good reason why it can't be done).

Happy new year,
Jim

messages.body_plain:
stan-mode is based off of emacs cc-mode, which has a very customizable indentation engine, which you can read about  here <http://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/ccmode/Indentation-Calculation.html#Indentation-Calculation>. It's based off of the syntatic class of the first element in the line, which in your example would be arglist-intro (you can find this using C-c C-s <http://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/ccmode/Syntactic-Symbols.html#Syntactic-Symbols>). You change the indentation rules using the variable c-offsets-alist <http://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/ccmode/c_002doffsets_002dalist.html#c_002doffsets_002dalist>. For your example, you'd want to add this to your init file. It will override the default indentation for lines beginning with arglist-intro.

> (add-hook 'stan-mode-hook
>  (setq c-offsets-alist
>   '("stan" (arglist-intro . +))))
